speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: STATEMENT ON 1970-71 CAPITAL BUDGET OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order that plans may be made and programs developed for the fiscal year 1970-71, the government has now approved the capital budget of the Farm Credit Corporation. There are certain aspects of this budget that will be of considerable interest to members of this House and to farmers across Canada.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Adjustment of production practices is taking place all across Canada. In the prairie provinces many farmers are currently shifting or planning to shift to the production of livestock as an alternative to producing grain for direct sale. In other parts of the country dairy farmers and others are facing decisions of the same nature. Such changes of enterprise must be carefully planned, with due regard for the long-term market prospects as well as other considerations such as the provision of buildings, machinery, and the alternative of farm rotation to meet the changing pattern. Such changes must also be properly financed on a long-term basis. I wish to confirm that the Farm Credit Corporation may provide long-term credit to farmers who wish to adjust their resource utilization to

January 22, 1970
Farm Credit Corporation better meet the market demands. The budget of the Farm Credit Corporation for the coming year has been adjusted to provide additional funds to meet the increase in demand which is expected for loans for this purpose in the coming fiscal year. The field officers of the Farm Credit Corporation can be a valuable source of information and assistance to farmers in these matters.
An additional feature of the new budget is that it will provide funds to permit farmers who find it necessary and desirable to refinance current liabilities. These loans will be made available to cereal grain producers operating viable farm businesses who under ordinary circumstances would be able to operate satisfactorily but whose ability to do so has been impaired by inability to market their grain and who thus may need to refinance short and intermediate-term liabilities over a longer term. Applications for such loans, of course, will be subject to the usual other criteria for loans from the corporation.
The corporation will take steps to inform farmers that this assistance is available to them.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON 1970-71 CAPITAL BUDGET OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Minister of Agriculture regarding the capital budget of the Farm Credit Corporation will certainly be studied with a great deal of interest by the agricultural industry across Canada.
His statement is very modest in tone when it says that "adjustment of production practices is taking place all across Canada." In essence what he is alluding to is the fact that the agricultural industry is staggering because of the lowest return it has experienced in its history.
Although the minister states that money will be made available for long-term loans for the provision of buildings, machinery and the alternative of farm rotation to assist in shifting production from grain to livestock, I think this program is weak. There are two apparent weaknesses which will be evident to the farmers immediately. First-and this concerns the west particularly-it is stated that loans will be made to cereal grain producers operating viable farm businesses who under ordinary circumstances would be able to operate satisfactorily but who may need to refinance short and intermediate-term liabilities over a longer term. This point will need some clarification on the part of the department because what the farmers need especially is not money to refinance short and inter-

mediate-term loans but immediate operating capital. I hope this will be taken into consideration.
The other weakness, Mr. Speaker, which I think is more apparent and is a major one, is the fact that the government is proceeding now to lend the farmers of this nation additional capital for the purpose of refinancing, which will put them further in debt. The weakness lies in the fact that the farmers of this nation are not aware of the long-term policy of the government regarding agriculture. It is of no value to refinance farmers with respect to a particular field of endeavour if it is long-term government policy to curtail the production of the essential products in which they are involved. It is a fact that many farmers have undertaken a tremendous amount of debt only to find there is no longer an economic market for the supplies produced and they are therefore unable to finance the debt.
Until the government is able to spell out its program in its entirety and say whether it is going to enter the field of supply management and under such a program curtail production to meet domestic requirements only, the Farm Credit Corporation will not be able to solve many of the problems farmers face today merely by granting long-term loans.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subtopic: STATEMENT ON 1970-71 CAPITAL BUDGET OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this program is, of course, another ad hoc approach to the problem that exists in Canada as a whole and in western Canada in particular. If the Farm Credit Corporation makes additional moneys available to the farmers, undoubtedly some of them will borrow.
One bad feature of the announcement is that nothing has been mentioned about adjusting interest rates to meet the probable ability of the farmer to pay. Apparently he is expected to borrow money at high interest rates for a long term.
The second weakness I wish to point out lies in the fact that we know changes are taking place in production patterns in western Canada. Indeed, some provinces are already assisting these changes; Manitoba and Saskatchewan are two examples. If money is now made available these changes probably will be accelerated. What is needed is an assessment of the market situation and the demand for various farm products. Some people may have to go out of grain production on a long-term basis. The question is, how much land should they take out of production? In a recent news-
January 22, 1970

letter the Department of Agriculture made an estimate of 20 million acres.
We have seen in the past crop year that a change in pricing and marketing practices has increased substantially the marketings of barley, a feed grain. What we need is an accurate assessment of the potential market for grain, feed grains and oilseeds in the years immediately ahead, and the probable absorption by the market of livestock production. Only on forecasts of this kind can the farmer make a rational judgment. That, of course, is the real basis of his problem. He must be able to make a rational judgment.
The government of Canada through the Department of Agriculture is making increased amounts of money available. If this money is utilized for types of production that will be in trouble in a few years, we shall not have solved the difficulty. Therefore I plead with the government and the Minister of Agriculture to get some people working on a long-range as well as an immediate-range program along the lines I have outlined so that the farmer may, hopefully, make intelligent decisions.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement seems interesting in many regards. However, one should also refer to a statement he made in Quebec on January 29, 1969, and I quote:
In many sectors ot agriculture, scientific progress is just beginning to be felt and to promise for the first time revolutionary innovations. The history of mankind teaches us that technology-
"Technology" is a very big word, and already we have begun to suffer from it. The statement goes on:
-is an international commodity. Gunpowder, a Chinese discovery, reached Europe like a train of powder, so to speak, and revolutionized the art of war.
Improvements in the field of agriculture may be due to experiments in genetics carried out in Mexico, in a laboratory in the United States, in Europe or elsewhere. Whatever their origin, their effects will finally be felt in Canadian agriculture. It is precisely the high-geared pace of technological developments that makes it so complicated to devise an agricultural policy.
We are given another proof today that we are living in an extremely complex world, when we read the following part of the minister's statement:
Adjustment of production practices is taking place all across Canada. In the Prairie provinces many farmers are currently shifting-

on the advice of experts I would imagine,
-or planning to shift to the production of livestock as an alternative to producing grain for direct sale.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
In the eastern provinces, learned economists, those who come up with solutions when we are in a complete state of stagnation, have advised our processed milk producers to take the same course of action. They said: "There are milk surpluses. Produce alternate goods. Take up cattle ranching." Then, in western and eastern Canada, farmers are encouraged to raise cattle. And when there is a meat surplus on the market, farmers will be blamed and told: You are the most stupid, because you are all producing the same goods. You alone are responsible. You produce too much beef, prices fall, bear your rate patiently.
In advocating this policy, the minister necessarily wanted to create new debts. Indeed, to undertake a new kind of production, the equipment must be changed. The new production will have to bear the burden of debts accumulated during a deficit period. This change of program will be called debt conversion in order to prolong the martyrdom which is the fate of farmers already burdened with terrible debts, while an appeal is made to them to have patience in these words: Wait, exercise patience, the situation will improve.
The minister is well aware that to make sure that eastern and western farmers can live reasonably and enjoy a fair share of the national revenue, prices must correspond to production. The minister knows it very well because he said it often and I congratulate him. I hope however that his memory is good. He said that the problem in 1966 was one of "cost-price", and the problem is still the same. We are in a squeeze, we are choking and we are trying to get out of that.
In my opinion, if we really want to improve the condition of eastern and western farmers, interest rates will have to go down so as to reduce the production cost and leave the producers with a small profit. It is thus that, in my opinion, we will be able to give to farmers a fair share of the national revenue.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT BY ANDRE SAUMIER- STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 18 last, at the

January 22, 1970
National Film Board
request of the Government Film Commissioner and Chairman of the National Film Board, I entrusted Mr. Andre Saumier with the task of making an analysis of the staff reductions planned by the management of the National Film Board as a result of the budgetary restrictions imposed by the government's austerity program. This appointment of a person outside the NFB seemed at the time to be the best way of studying the difficulties between the board's top management and its production staff arising from the reductions announced for December 15, 1969. The report was submitted to the commissioner on January 15 and I am tabling it today, together with the commissioner's comments.
The primary finding of the report is that the board is not threatened with imminent paralysis, as certain persons have given to understand during the past few weeks. It is true that its over-all production level for the 1970-71 fiscal year is to be reduced to what it was in 1964-65; nevertheless, this represents a net budget of $10 million, which is far from negligible.

In order to gain a proper perspective, the National Film Board's activities must be viewed within the broader and more realistic context of the government's activities as a whole in the field of cinematography; here I should like to emphasize the continuous growth in this sector and the unremitting attention given to it by the Secretary of State. The Board's present difficulties should not hide the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or of the Canadian Film Development Corporation. In 1964, the CBC spent the sum of $9,500,000 on the production of films for television; in 1970-71, this sum will be $13,000,000.
In 1964, there was no such thing as the Film Development Corporation; during its first year of existence (1968-69) it invested $366,639 in the production of 20 feature films and made awards amounting to $100,000. In 1970-71 it plans to invest a total of 2.5 million in Canada's film industry.
In addition to this, the government is negotiating co-production agreements with a number of countries with a view to helping Canadian films gain admission to the international market. Thus it is obvious that the government is taking an ever-increasing interest in the film industry as a whole, and that NFB activities must from now on be considered in this global context.

The question that must be confronted is this: what should be the role of each of the institutions involved in this over-all activity and what relations should they have with one another? This question has been under consideration for several months now and we hope to offer an answer before the present session comes to an end.
Furthermore, the difficulties the NFB is now experiencing are forcing it to take a hard look at its structures and policy, having regard both to present-day realities in the realm of cinematography and budget restrictions. I feel certain that the Board will have no trouble finding its place in this new expanded context and that its contribution therein will continue to be essential. Obviously, the transition must take place with minimum delay while respecting the fundamental integrity of the organization itself.

It is also essential that following the present difficulties the number of inevitable layoffs among the production staff be kept to a minimum. This objective has been given particular attention. I have been assured today by the management of the board that the number of lay-offs on the English production side, which was to have been 37, will be reduced to 32 and that 12 of those affected will receive a one-year termination notice instead of the usual three months. Following these lay-offs there will be 146 employees in the English production unit and 70 in the French production unit. It is therefore obvious that the National Film Board's vital creative staff will be maintained. Its development will be assured by a dynamic new definition of its role, and the unique contribution it has to make to the cultural life of Canada will also be assured.

Mr. Speaker, there are two initial comments I should like to make in connection with the Saumier report. The report came into my hands only just before the opening of the sitting this afternoon, so I have only been able to peruse it briefly.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
On the basis of that perusal, I can say that it is an excellent report and one which goes far beyond the original terms of reference, which were to inquire into the dismissals at the National Film Board. Mr. Saumier has gone far beyond an examination of that immediate problem and in the process has
January 22, 1970

given us a very excellent outline of the problems that beseige and beset not only the National Film Board operations but also the whole cinematography industry in Canada. Actually most of these difficulties were known prior to the tabling of the report because the problems were discussed as recently as a year ago by the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, which came to the same conclusions.
In addition to Mr. Saumier's outline of the broad problems in his report, he pointed out the immediate crisis which precipitated the demonstration on Parliament Hill by employees of the NFB, and which eventually forced the government to look into the matter, arose from the implementation of the current austerity program in a rather crude and blunt fashion. I am sure this same criticism can be made of the application of the austerity program in other departments and government activities.
Those of us who took the trouble to meet with the employees of the National Film Board when they were on Parliament Hill just before Christmas heard them outline the main difficulties that are again enumerated in the report. Mr. Norman McLaren, one of the most creative individuals not only in the industry in Canada but throughout the world, was one of the spokesmen on that occasion. The substance of the points made was that creative talents were going to suffer from the blunt application of government austerity. It was said that the English division of the National Film Board was going to be starved under the application of the austerity program. It was also said that there was an emphasis on management at the expense of production and creative talent in the National Film Board.
The report, as the Secretary of State has indicated, has reaffirmed these comments and criticisms made by representatives of the National Film Board early in December, and already some corrective action is to be taken to deal with this difficulty. With reference to management problems it is worth while to note that on page two Mr. Saumier emphasized that difficulty in these words:
It should be emphasized here that the senior management of the board, located moreover far from the capital, had scant knowledge of the mysterious workings of government in Ottawa.
He is not the only one who has that difficulty, Mr. Speaker, because even those of us in this House could make the same observation. This statement indicates that the highly
National Film Board
controversial move of the NFB in the 1950's from the capital to Montreal was a mistake, as many said at that time, and is perhaps one of the major reasons for the worsening position of that branch of government service.
The main difficulty, which should be emphasized in respect of the broad perspective, that is, other than the immediate crisis caused by austerity, has been pointed out in Mr. Saumier's report in these words:
There does not exist at the present a comprehensive federal government policy with regard to information or cultural affairs.
He enlarges on that general criticism by saying that the major difficulty in the whole field of cinematography and audio-visual communications is that there is no comprehensive federal government policy regarding information on cultural affairs. This not only affects the operations of the National Film Board but also deeply involves the private sector of the industry. I remind hon. members that during a series of meetings of the committee last year it was pointed out to us that the whole audio-visual industry in Canada, the motion picture industry and the cinematography industry are in a state of crisis at the present time and as a result are forming a Canadian motion picture academy in an attempt to come to grips with the problem. Much more expeditious and vigorous action on the part of the government is required to find a solution than such palliatives as the establishment of the Canadian Film Development Corporation and some of the other measures the Secretary of State has referred to in his brief statement this afternoon. In particular we will have to deal with the invasion of the motion picture industry by that great republic to the south of us. This represents one of the main areas of difficulty.
Finally, Mr. Saumier also dealt with another aspect which I think is of primary importance. If the objective outlined by the Secretary of State is to be realized, namely, to make the National Film Board more visible, we must remember that one result of the present austerity program has been to cut out free distribution of National Film Board productions to community film councils. The NFB has been one of the main sources of adult education in the more outlying parts of the country. I urge the Secretary of State, as does the Saumier report, to review this matter carefully. It is quite possible that in this regard the government is being penny wise and pound foolish.

Mr. Speaker, the National Film Board, as members of this House know, has over the years built up an international reputation. It has won awards at film festivals throughout the world. It has built up a devoted following in Canada. Co-operatives, labour unions, home and school associations and community groups of all types have used National Film Board productions extensively. It is little comfort to the Film Board and its employees to be told by the Secretary of State that there has been an expansion in the production of films financed by the government through the CBC and the new corporation which finances film-making by private companies.
The Film Board is faced with a reduction in staff, despite the slight modifications announced by the minister, by 100 people in the next couple of months. Of these a very substantial number, in fact the largest percentage, will come from the English production division. In addition, the user fees which the Film Board has instituted as a result of the austerity forced upon it by the government will have a bad result. I know that hon. members and the minister have received representations from various groups in all parts of Canada that they cannot afford the user fees and will be forced to curtail sharply or discontinue completely the use of films they have been procuring from the Film Board. So we are faced with a further reduction in staff of possibly another 50 people who work in the distribution field if the use of films produced by the board is cut substantially.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Let me tell the minister that in spite of his kind words today there is panic in the National Film Board and morale has dropped to an all-time low with the result that people are going to leave just as quickly as they can find something else to do. It is an interesting commentary on this government that the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State, who came into public life with a reputation for being intellectuals and persons of culture, are in charge of a government which is going to preside over the virtual demise of the National Film Board and a very sharp reduction in the creative facilities of the CBC. That is something which ought to be noted very carefully.
There is one other point I must put on the record and I hope the minister will take note of it. In his report Mr. Saumier points out that as a result of the planned cutbacks in

English language production the staff will be reduced to a level of 90 per cent of what it was in 1964-65 and that on the French language production side the staff will be 142 per cent of what it was in 1964-65. All of us in this group come from constituencies whose people are largely English-speaking. We have tried very hard to explain to our constituents and the people of Canada why the proposals of the government to increase the use of the French language and to make it easier for people whose mother tongue is French to work for the government and live in all parts of Canada are necessary in order to maintain this country as one nation. But I say to the minister that such an unfair cutback on the English production side will make it very difficult for us to explain that kind of policy to our constituents.

Mr. Speaker, in his statement to the House about Mr. Andre Saumier's report on the analysis of the staff reductions planned by the management of the National Film Board, the minister said:
-The Board's present difficulties should not hide the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or of the Canadian Film Development Corporation.
The minister states clearly that three agencies financed by the government are concerned with the distribution of films produced in Canada and abroad. The minister added:
In 1964, the C.B.C. spent the sum of $9,500,000 on the production of films for television; in 1970-71, this sum will be $13,000,000.

Mr. Speaker, anyone who looks at the television films produced by the C.B.C. and compares them to those produced by the N.F.B. can readily see how superior the latter are to the educational films made by the C.B.C. for the people of Canada. As a matter of fact, the N.F.B. seeks to educate Canadians, instead of brainwashing them as the C.B.C. does. Why, then, should appropriations for the C.B.C. be considerably increased while those of the N.F.B. are being reduced.
Each time I have had occasion to view a television film produced by the N.F.B., I was aware that it was of a highly educational nature. For instance, we are informed about the North-West Territories and various other areas of Canada.
January 22, 1970

And the C.B.C., what kind of film does it make in Canada? I will recall in that respect that, during the Christmas season, it showed a one-hour telecast produced in an Old People's Home in Montreal and during which Robert Charlebois swore like blazes for an hour, the whole program being sponsored by the C.B.C.
If one considers the type of films made by the C.B.C. about our own area, Abitibi, when we are shown uninhabited shanties to illustrate the poverty which is rampant over there, one concludes that there is no need for the C.B.C. to go to Abitibi in order to produce such feats. Mr. Speaker, the government should not reduce appropriations to the N.F.B. but rather help this organization more generously than it does now the C.B.C. which does not fulfill its mission, which is to further the general welfare of the people.

There is a pattern of ship loss in Arctic waters. The losses occur usually when a ship becomes wedged and immovable in the ice. Pressure builds, either by tide or by winds. The ship is crushed and, when released, sinks.
The ecological disaster of a 250,000-ton supertanker spilling crude oil into waters of 27 to 30 degrees fahrenheit strains the imagination. It certainly exceeds our knowledge. The Canadian government, to its discredit, has not even yet undertaken tests of Prudhoe Bay crude oil action under these circumstances. Only during the recent visit of the parliamentary committee to the north did the Fisheries Research Board send its first researcher to those waters to make preliminary investigations.
The suggestions are that crude oil at temperatures below the freshwater freezing mark will form a gelatinous mass which, when deposited on shorelines, may remain for decades and possibly for a century. The lethal effects upon marine life (another subject on which our government remains ignorant and apparently indifferent) are beyond calculation. However, it is recognized that many crude oils contain substances as lethal as DDT. A quarter-million ton tanker could contain killing chemical substances of a scope never inflicted before on any ecology of the world. The Arctic skein of life is probably the least suited to withstand pollution on this gargantuan scale.
I pause here in the quotation to express concern for the people who depend on the land and the waters of the north for their very livelihood, to express concern for the native people, the Indians and the Eskimos who stand the risk of being exploited by commercial plunderers before they can be said to have even lived. Their living conditions are still wretched. They have the highest mortal.ty rate among Canada's native people. I continue the quotation:
In her national interest-the prime concern of any nation's government-Canada must control any oil shipments through the Northwest Passage.
We could not deny the rights of innocent passage from one ocean to another if technology has made this possible. But the determination of what constitutes innocent passage must be ours. We are the nation vitally concerned. The determination of which ships are safe and which are dangerously unfit cannot be left to Humble Oil or any of the international companies. It cannot be left to a foreign power. It cannot be left to the United Nations. The Canadian Arctic is the concern of Canadians, unless we choose to abrogate that responsibility.
If enough Canadians know the facts, I don't think they'll choose to ignore this challenge.
We have ample right to claim the waters within the Arctic Archipelago as our own. We have rights of discovery, of continuous occupation, and we have rights by reason that this is a continuous archipelago of the Hinterland doctrine. Ours is not an ocean archipelago, comparable with Indonesia where international shipping has passed for millennia, beginning with Chinese explorers. The Arctic islands are an extension of the Canadian continental land mass and our internationally recognized control of the Labrador coast and of Hudson Bay extends logically and naturally into the High Arctic Islands.
We have further rights. The Arctic and Antarctic seas are not like all others. They are frozen for much of the year. The definition between land and water is sometimes detectable only by instruments. At least one authority has stated that a ship frozen in Arctic seas, far from land and communicating with land only by surface vehicle, is more effectively a part of the Canadian land mass than is a ship at anchor in one of our southern harbours.
For these and other reasons, I am convinced that the waters within the archipelago have been Canadian, are now Canadian and must remain exclusively Canadian.
As I mentioned before, Mr. Speaker, I am not the author of those words. They are the thoughts of the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin, expressed in an article.

speechtext:
Much of our concern lor the Arctic involves the question of pollution. We now believe that Canada should be responsible for effective control in this area. It cannot be left to other powers or the United Nations. What do we know about the effects of pollution in the north? We may know something of its effects on the Ottawa River, though I really wonder, but even so, we do not seem to know how to provide the leadership to prevent this man-made mutilation of our environment which is happening on our doorstep.
But concern there is on pollution, and we need to know more. The Committee on Northern Development has made such a recommendation. I refer you to the sinking in Viscount Melville Sound on August 21, 1969 of the Panarctic barges, "Learmouth" and "John A. Norberg". The latter was loaded at the time with 470,000 gallons of bulk oil, mostly Arctic diesel. The Department of Transport reported a week after the sinking that:
The diesel oil spilled into the sea is a relatively light distillate and as a result, long lasting pollution will not occur.
I quote now from the circular published by The Arctic Circle, Ottawa, dated November, 1969, which reads:
Crude oil certainly makes a more obvious and unsightly mess than diesel oil. Reports indicate, however, that diesel oil is much more toxic than crude oil. For example, the Smithsonian Institution Centre for Short-lived Phenomena records (in Marine Pollution Bulletin, No. 16, October, 1969) that an estimated leakage of only 10,000 gallons of No. 2 diesel oil from the barge "Florida" off the coast of Massachusetts, on 17 and 18 September caused "extensive mortality to marine life-At least 24 species of fin-fish are dying in large numbers- scallops are hardest hit. Even in West Falmouth Harbour where there is no visual or olfactory evidence of oil, they are dying by the thousand."
It must be made clear that these Arctic waters and straits are Canadian and will remain Canadian. The Northwest Passage is not an international strait because there have been virtually no passages of the sort required in the past centuries to establish it as anything other than Canadian waters. It has been said before, and bears repeating, that the passage is not an international one because it is not customarily and cannot customarily be used as an international strait.

Without Canadian sovereignty we cannot control pollution, and we cannot guard against wicked exploitation of the north and its people.
At this stage I do not know what antipollution measures the government envisages for the north or how these will be controlled. It may be they have huge reserves of straw from the prairies just waiting to be used to sop up spilled oil. Perhaps a contract has already been signed for a ten-year supply of detergent. I just hope that if the Arctic waters are to be open to every Tom, Dick or Harry, the planned measures to combat pollution will be adequate.
The risk of a Torrey Canyon disaster hangs over all of our heads today and the best insurance policy in the world would not and could not possibly compensate for the damage to our environment if a disaster of the Torrey Canyon magnitude happened in the north. A disaster of that proportion would upset the delicate balance of nature in the north and may lead to complete ecological breakdown in the Arctic. It could reach out to every man, woman and child on this earth.
Sovereign control of the Arctic does not imply interference with innocent and peaceful passage. I want to make this clear, Mr. Speaker, that as far as I am concerned I welcome marine traffic through the straits as I think it will encourage development in that area. However, Canada must ultimately decide what constitutes innocent passage and must have the right to make and enforce regulations which protect our national interest.
e (3:10 p.m.)
Because of your positive and progressive ruling, Mr. Speaker, the committees of this House have been given an important role. Their reports are that much more important because of the close attention that these committees can pay to detail. These are committees of the House, and not instruments of government. We have before us the recommendations of one such committee which, I believe, expresses the concern of all thinking Canadians. To vote against this motion or to further stall its consideration by this House is a vote against Canada, a vote against claims of Canadian sovereignty in northern lands and waters rightfully ours, and a vote against humanity itself.

But, Mr. Speaker, I am dealing with the possible results of a decision.
It should be realized that this committee report, as well as the one brought down last year, contains more than a statement on Arctic sovereignty or what might be called a statement of principle; these reports were very detailed and committed the cabinet and the government to, among other things, the expenditure of money. I doubt very much the propriety of this course.
I do not oppose a movement towards a congressional system of government.
I do not oppose the adoption of a congressional system which would give greater powers to committees and which would bring many changes to Parliament. Nevertheless, neither I nor the Canadian people are prepared yet to abandon the idea of cabinet responsibility.
The committee may recommend the expenditure of money but is not charged with providing it. Only this House has the power to provide money and, according to my understanding, it is the cabinet that initiates such expenditures before the House.
Hon. members who have read this report carefully will no doubt note that it was not written in the usual style of committee reports, in which it is usually stated that "the government should consider the advisability" of doing this and that or, that the committee recommends such and such a general course of action. This report does not recommend that the government should study the advisability of do ng such and such a thing merely because the members of the committee believe it should be done in that way.
Let us see what the cabinet would be committed to by way of the expenditure of money if there were concurrence in this committee report. On page 210 of Votes and Proceedings of December 16, we find the following:
The Committee recommends that appropriate agencies of the Government move immediately to

conduct research in the Arctic to gather information on the following:
(A)	Physical properties of crude oils and other hydrocarbons in cold waters, the dynamics of their dispersion, and their persistence in water and on and under ice;
(B)	The toxicity of various hydrocarbons to plant and animal life;

Your Committee recommends-
(A)	An operational research study to determine polution safeguards to be required of oil tankers and pollutant-carrying maritime traffic in Arctic and North Atlantic waters;
(B)	A research project into the effect of oil and other chemical pollutants on the marine biology and ecology of the cold waters of the Arctic and North Atlantic Oceans;
(C)	A supporting programme aimed at developing improved methods combatting pollution in low temperature waters.
In last year's report, the committee also urged the government to take prompt action to establish our Arctic sovereignty. There was no motion for concurrence in that report which also contained recommendations, I believe, with respect to increased government spending.
Although I do not have last year's report before me, I can recall that it urged the government to spend more money on certain matters. One was that it spend more money on Indian Centres.
May I say that I am not retreating from my previous position. I still think it was wise for this committee to recommend what it recommended. My mind has not been changed. Nevertheless, I urge members of this House to consider carefully what will happen if they give to committees the power, apparently, to put the Canadian cabinet in a straitjacket.

I wish to open my remarks with a statement that was made in 1963 to the Canadian Political Science Conference in Quebec. The quotation is from a speech by Gordon W. Smith and reads as follows:
Canadians might be a little less complacent about the vast northern areas shown in bright red on Mercator's familiar projection if they appreciated fully the tribulations that accompanied the acquisition of it-
I want to underline these words as best I can:
-and if they understood that with little more ineptitude, or a little less luck on our part, or a little more aggressive competition from some other statutes, they might not have become ours.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, he was referring to our land areas of the High Arctic, the Territories and the Yukon.
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
Until very recent years, these areas were our only real concern in the north. I do not think many of us were concerned about water.
We are by no means a xenophobic nation. I do not think anyone has ever wanted to seal those waters against the legitimate commerce of the world.
I feel we have not studied the fish resources adequately, but we have s.udied them to some degree. This study has not been extensive since the whalers moved out from their operations early in the century.
There did not appear to be such urgency in the declaration of sovereignty over the waters, providing we had full and untrammelled sovereignty over the land areas which, according to any authority I have been able to find, we have, and providing we had full access to the resources of the seabed which again according to any authority I could find, we do have.
Then, whether we liked it or not, technology overtook us and oil was discovered at Prudhoe Bay.
Another big pool has been discovered by Imperial Oil at the mouth of the Mackenzie and in the High Arctic there is the Panarctic consortium partially supported by the government and partly by private money. There can be little doubt that that consortium has a handful of kings and aces in its search for another pool of oil in the High Arctic.
This oil, as well as oil that will be found, must somehow be moved to market.
In the search for efficient transportation methods the Humble Oil Company, in association with some other companies, undertook a daring and welcome experiment.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we can shrug off or evade the challenge of modern technology. We have to meet it head on.
I congratulate that company for its initia' ive in testing whether an ice-strengthened ship could operate regularly through the ice of the northwest passage.
This experiment has proven to be less than a complete success, although it has undoubtedly added a great deal to our knowledge of ice and Arctic conditions.
Perhaps I do not need to belabour this point because I think it is generally recognized by all hon. members-the perils associated with transportation of crude oil or any hydrocarbon through ice filled waters of the north verges on the intolerable. I do not suggest they are completely intolerable, because
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic the problems technology presents to us in one form it can meet us with solutions for in another form. However, as yet it has not provided a solution to this problem.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk) quoted from an article which I wrote recently. The common peril of ships in the Arctic has always been to be besieged by the ice, to be crushed by the ice and to sink.
The S.S. Manhattan returned with a hole in her side large enough to drive a truck through, even though the ice conditions in that area were the easiest in many years. In connection with tankers moving through the archipelago, on the surface or under the sea, I might point out that there is a study under way and plans are being drawn which may or may not come to fruition for 40,000 or 50,000 ton submarine tankers operating under the ice.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The peril under the ice does not differ entirely from the peril to which surface vessels are exposed.
Someone must control this movement through the passage.
We must be satisfied that the ships are safe and that they are not designed in such a way as would permit them to be crushed, losing their cargoes.
Alternatively, we must he confident that technology has provided a means for the total neutralization of oil cargoes or their total destruction in the event of shipwreck. To the best of my knowledge, technology has not yet provided us with these means.
The important point-one which was well made by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and I expect to hear it made again in the House today-is who will be responsible for doing this?
Logically, the responsibility not only on behalf of Canada but on behalf of the whole world community falls directly upon this nation and upon this government.
If we are not sufficiently concerned about the danger of the greatest ecological disaster in human history befalling the Arctic it is idle to expect that other nations will assume this concern for us. Their attitude will to a large degree be determined by our attitude, because these are our waters and our islands.
May I ask you how much time I have left, Mr. Speaker? I am sorry, but I have lost track of the hand of the clock.

Thank you. Of course, we are not alone in our concern about the danger of pollution.
I am not suggesting that the United States or any other of our neighbouring nations are indifferent to it. In fact, it is my understanding that on the day following the address given by the Prime Minister on leader's day, the United States government communicated with our embassy in Washington expressing support for his views about the need for measures to control possible pollution in the north.
But again-and this cannot be said too often-the need for concern is primarily ours.
It may be suggested in some quarters that there is a reasonable basis for the statement by the Canadian government that no further pronouncements are necessary because, after all, these are our waters, and they are accepted as being ours by the world community as a matter of course. Unfortunately, it is not necessarily accepted by the world community as a matter of course, and in this connection I wish to deal for a few moments with an article which appeared in the White Horse Star and was reprinted in the Edmonton Journal.
The writer is Mr. Peter Calamai of the Southam News Service and the article is important because it reflects the attitude of at least one group of Americans who are concerned about this matter and the repercussions do not bode good for us. I shall read a few paragraphs.
Boston. The controversial use of the Northwest Passage to ship oil from Alaska was discussed here Friday-without beneflt of any Canadian participation and with only fleeting reference to the fears of a disastrous oil spill.
U.S. and Humble Oil officials in the discussion panel at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science here also carefully skirted the question of Arctic sovereignty.
Russell Venn, Humble vice-president who was aboard the tanker Manhattan for part of its historic September crossing of the passage, said he was sure Canada would not try to impose fees on U.S. oil companies making use of Arctic waters.
In response to a question about ownership of the waters around Banks Island-a key piece of land in any Northwest Passage-Mr. Venn said the Canadian government was leary of publicly renouncing any claims on the waters because then the ownership of seabed mineral wealth would be calculated from the Canadian continental coastline rather than from the islands.
Because Canada wanted to be able to export natural gas and other products to the United States without paying tariffs it was unlikely that the Canadian government would attempt to impose any economic restraints-
January 22, 1970

The article continued:
Mr. Venn told his audience that the Manhattan was visited by "a bunch of MPs."
"They were very worried about sovereignty; I figure that must have been among the more liberal ones in the bunch," he said.
Members of the Commons Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development greeted the Manhattan at Resolute Bay on Cornwallis Island.
There was no mention from any of the three speakers of the environmental threat of an oil spill in the Arctic. When an audience member raised the problem at the end of the three-hour session, Mr. Venn said Humble had done research on the techniques of cleaning up such a spill. "I think we can avoid them."
I have already praised Humble Oil for their initiative in making this scientific experiment and I do not retract those words. But what took place at that conference does not reflect the concern which should be felt for the preservation and safety of the Canadian Arctic.

Officials of the Humble Oil Company do not speak United States government policy, I recognize this. But their approach is one more reason for the Canadian government to make an early statement on the matter in order that the attitude of any foreign companies may not stand up.
This casual, I might even say cavalier, attitude to the near-intolerable threat posed by tankers going through the passage calls out for a response from this country.
I should like to deal briefly with the position of the United States government on this matter.
It is not entirely clear to me.
I find that the statements made on the subject are sometimes a trifle conflicting.
Let me say this: I think the Americans might well ask themselves which nation in the world has been America's best friend for the longest time.
I suggest it is not in the best interest of the United States that the waters of the Northwest Passage should be regarded as high seas any more than such a declaration about the Panama Canal would be in their interest.
Do they want these waters supervised by their main trading partner, their military ally and faithful friend, or do they want them to become an international no man's land with all the security risks which might be entailed?
I hope that any American who might speak impulsively about the freedom of the seas in connection with this matter will first pause and consider the repercussions.
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
As to the Canadian legal position, I have more references here than time will allow me to read, but there is one to which I should like to draw attention because hon. members may not be familiar with it.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, urged that we should make a clear and direct claim to the Arctic, including the icy portions, not only because of the risk of foreign control but because he was concerned about the possibility of the establishment of IBM's on the ice to the detriment of Canada's position.
I intend to quote another speaker, one who can, I think, be considered an expert on this subject-Dean George Curtis of UBC. Dean Curtis is one of those who has represented Canada at international conferences on these matters.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Dean George Curtis was an adviser to the Canadian government in the early 1950's regarding the DEW line construction and matters concerning Canadian sovereignty.
He spoke briefly to the Canadian Bar convention here in Ottawa last summer.
He was not reported and what I give you is a paraphrase of his remarks. I can assure you that this is correct as I have checked it with him by telephone.
He made three points:
First, he thought the Norwegian decision as confirmed by the Geneva conference made it feasible for Canada to lay claim to the waters within a system of headland to headland straight base lines.
Second, he felt it was extremely important to do this in order to protect the ecology of the High Arctic and that this was a responsibility that Canada had in her own interest and in the interest of the world at large.
Finally, he said, and again I am paraphrasing him, that if this area were left in the realm of the high seas there would be no protection.
As to the extension of a state's power beyond its shores to control pollution or the threat of pollution, I refer to one current and one recent incident in the United States which indicate that the United States fully understands the necessity for this.
The United States has set one or two precedents.
One precedent, and this is a small matter, but significant, concerned the salvage of a
2690	COMMONS
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic Liberian oil tanker in January 1968 about 400 miles off the coast of Washington.
The Vancouver Island Salvage Company sent two tugs out to pick up an oil tanker which was on fire. The fire burned out but there was still some oil in her holds.
The Sudbury II and the Island Monarch were the two tugs.
As they brought her in, heading for Vancouver Island and nearing the United States coastline, the officers were informed by the United States through its coast guard that they could not bring that ship within 50 miles of the United States coastline.
I do not blame the United States in the least for making such a decision. I think that was quite wise. But it certainly indicates United States acquiescence to the principle that a coastal state has the right to such controls beyond what are normally considered to be territorial waters.
Let me refer hon. members to two bills, one before the United States House of Representatives and the other before the United States Senate. They are roughly of the same intent although there are some differences between them.
A joint committee of those two houses is now attempting to meld them into a single bill for presentation and presumably for passage.
If adopted they will give the United States the right to fine companies for pollution of sea water and to control the activities of vessels which might pollute these waters. This is quite a comprehensive piece of legislation.
The point which I draw to the attention of hon. members is that the United States by this legislation, if it is passed, does not adopt this right in terms of the 3-mile limit to which they adhere today in international discussions.
The United States legislation would apply to the 3-mile limit and the contiguous area; that extra nine miles, bringing it to an effective 12-mile limit.
If nothing else, I hope the Canadian government can move quickly to establish the 12-mile limit for Canada instead of the present 3 plus 9 mile limit. But it is possible, probable perhaps, that the 3 plus 9 miles is sufficient for our purposes after drawing the base lines.
I regret I do not have time to pursue that matter.
There are one or two other matters which I may have time to bring to the attention of the House.
DEBATES	January 22, 1970
I should like to touch very briefly on the attitude of the Soviet government and quote from Mr. Lakhtine who wrote some time ago in the American Journal of International Law. He summarized his points as follows:
(1)	Polar states wield sovereignty over sea regions covered with ice, according to their sectors of attraction.
(2)	Littoral states wield sovereignty over land locked seas free from ice, and over gulfs and bays.
(3)	Littoral states are entitled to a somewhat limited sovereignty over all remaining sea regions free from ice, as well as over territorial waters, maritime belts and waters between islands according to their sectors of attraction.
If action by the Canadian government should lead to a dispute in any international court I do not think the mighty Soviet Union would be in a very good position to oppose the Canadian government's position in establishing our sovereign control over the waters of the passage.
In closing, and for the sake of clarity, let me say I hope that nothing I have said here has conveyed the impression that I should like to see Canada seal the Northwest Passage.
Nothing could be further from my thoughts.
We, as Canadians, should look forward hopefully to a day when technology provides ships which will move much of the commerce of the world across the north of Canada.
However, Mr. Speaker, we must take the authority to control that shipping which we consider dangerous.
At the Geneva conference of 1958 there was adopted a definition of innocent passage, and innocent passage is certainly what we should offer to the world, together with our declaration of sovereignty over those waters.
Innocent passage may generally apply not only to territorial waters or to internal waters but may apply also to waters recently enclosed by base lines, such as in the Norwegian decision.
Generally, innocent passage provides that ships may pass through waters providing three things; they are not a threat to the security of the nation involved; that they are not a threat to the peace of the nation involved and, quite adequate for our purposes in the north, that they are not a threat to the good order of the nation involved.
There is no national court or body of the United Nations, in my opinion, that could possibly accept the notion that the spillage of a quarter of a million tons of crude oil in Canada's north would not be a threat to the good order of our country.

January 22, 1970

I maintain that our legal opinion, based on a number of references for recognizing authority, is sound and that our view should now be heard internationally.
I thank all hon. members for their courteous attention.

Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to congratulate the mover of this motion for concurrence in the report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I think he has rendered a genuine service to the House by insisting through his motion that this report from an important committee of the House be discussed. Reports of committees should be discussed and a decision should be taken on them by the House. I have long thought that there should be some change in our standing orders to the effect that all committee reports would have to be called within a certain period of time. The length of time that such reports might be discussed could be limited by allowing one speaker from each party, or by some other limitation. When they could be called might be established by the house leaders.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I might point out that if we allow, as we have been doing, the reports of committees merely to die on the Order Paper the work of these committees will become meaningless. The members who do not belong to those committees will have no opportunity to express their opinions regarding the matters which are contained in committee reports. The Prime Minister has talked a great deal about participatory democracy. If there is to be adequate participation in the democratic process by members of Parliament they must not only have an opportunity to discuss important public questions in depth, but must also be assured that the recommendations they make will be discussed by the House- not necessarily adopted by the House but at least discussed by the House and either amended, sent back to the committee or endorsed.
If I may, I should like to congratulate the members of the committee whose report we are now discussing for their ringing and forthright declaration regarding Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic Archipelago. What they have said needed to be said. I am glad it has been said in such forthright language. The whole kernel of our case is summed up
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic in three paragraphs. I think I should read them. At page 6 the report reads as follows:
Your Committee considers that the waters lying between the islands of the Arctic Archipelago have been, and are, subject to Canadian Sovereignty historically, geographically and geologically.
The imminent prospect of maritime oil tanker traffic through the Arctic Archipelago and the potential threat such traffic poses to Canada's Arctic environment makes it imperative to Canada's national interest that the Government of Canada take whatever steps are necessary, consistent with international law, to assure recognition of Canadian Sovereignty by all vessels, surface and submarine, passing through the Arctic Archipelago.
Your Committee recommends that the Government of Canada indicate to the world, without delay, that vessels, surface and submarine, passing through Canada's Arctic Archipelago are and shall be subject to the sovereign control and regulation of Canada.
A few moments ago while the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) was speaking a cabinet minister said "What is the debate for". The answer is simple. The debate is to give the members of this House an opportunity to endorse unanimously and enthusiastically this declaration of Canada's sovereignty over the Arctic Archipelago.

I must confess, sir, it is difficult for me to understand the government's reluctance to have the report of this committee discussed and approved in the House of Commons. The problem of Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic will not go away merely by being ignored. Quiet diplomacy is not likely to bring a solution. As a matter of fact, it is more likely to raise a doubt in the minds of Canadians and to encourage those governments which are desirous of claiming some vested interest in the far north.
Canadians do not want another Alaskan panhandle and they do not want Parliament to refrain from making a forthright declaration of Canada's legitimate rights to the Arctic Archipelago. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), in statements made outside the House, seeks to excuse his delaying action by the statement that the matter is under discussion by the government and that debate at this time would be premature. This government has been in office since April, 1963. Surely, by this time it has formulated a policy in respect of Canada's position vis-a-vis the Arctic regions. Previous administrations have been much more forthright. I will discuss later on the statement made by Canada in 1946 through Mr. Pear-

We must leave no doubt about our active occupation and exercise of our sovereignty in these northern lands right up to the pole.

That is what he said-"lands". I shall deal with waters as well. The minister points out that Mr. St. Laurent said "lands right up the the pole". Mr. Pearson, in 1946, talked about more than lands. I shall come to that in a moment. I think, in the new developing field of international law, Canada must assert its position and justify its claims. In an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of September 18, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) who just interjected, was quoted as saying:
-if it were (possible to obtain anything at all by unilateral declaration of intention) there would, of course, be international anarchy.
That is exactly the situation in the world today. With regard to territorial waters, only some 20 per cent of the nations of the world have established a 12-mile limit. More than 25 per cent still are on the 3-mile limit. Others have various figures. Three countries, Peru, Chile and Ecuador, have established a 200-mile limit for fishing purposes. What has happened in this new field of law of the sea has been that coastal states have made unilateral declarations. Those declarations, if objected to, have gone to the courts. As a result of the decisions in the courts, and as a result of conferences on the law of the sea, treaties and conventions have been established. The responsibility for making the assertion of sovereignty lies with the government of this country.
I should like to point out that Canada has good precedents in international law for its claim of sovereignty over the Arctic Archipelago. So far, no nation has ever questioned Canada's sovereignty over the islands between the mainland and the North Pole. The question at issue is whether the waters between these islands come exclusively under Canadian jurisdiction. I am not a lawyer, but through reading articles by lawyers in this field it becomes increasingly clear what happens is that out of precedents doctrines are built up and finally conventions are arrived at. There are three doctrines which to me as

a layman make very clear the justification for Canada making a declaration of sovereignty. The first is what is commonly called the sector claim doctrine. In 1946, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, who at that time was the Canadian ambassador to Washington, reasserted the sector claim which Canada had made as far back as 1908, which claim included all land, water and ice up to the pole. The Soviet Union still maintains this extensive sector claim which it first propounded back in 1926 and which it interprets as including not only lands within the sector but also ice, water and air space.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The other doctrine which has come to be recognized is the base line system, whereby a nation draws straight lines from headland to headland and claims all the waters within those lines. This system was first adopted by Norway, and was upheld in the well known fisheries case by the International Court of Justice in 1951. At the Geneva Conference on the law of the sea, this system was approved and incorporated in the convention of 1958, and has now become accepted as part of international law.
The third doctrine is that of the continental shelf, which was propounded by President Truman of the United States, who proclaimed that the resources of the subsoil and seabed of the continental shelf adjacent to a country's shores belonged to that nation. This principle was accepted and incorporated into an international convention at the United Nations Geneva Conference on the Law of the Sea in 1958. This convention specifies that a coastal state has the sovereign right to exploit the resources of its continental shelf lying adjacent to its coasts at a depth of 200 metres or less, and to a greater depth if exploitation proves feasible.
Some reference has already been made to the statements made by Professor Maxwell Cohen, the Dean of Law at McGill University. I noticed in an article which he wrote some time ago that he dealt with this matter, and I would like to quote just a paragraph from it:
And recent marine geology and cartography in the Arctic confirm that almost the entire archipelago and its waters are part of a shelf system within such average water depths except for one or two trenches and in deeper Lancaster Sound. There is therefore no doubt of exclusive Canadian control of the seabed beneath the entire waters area within the archipelago except for some limited geological aberrations where the depths exceed continental shelf standards. And even here there is a growing concept of claims to the continental slope to justify exclusive exploitation at greater depths.
January 22, 1970	COMMONS
I was glad to note that the committee, after examining the representations and the evidence given by Professor Cohen, had this to say in its report:
Your committee rejects the suggestion that an international waterway exists through the Canadian Arctic archipelago.
And later on in its report the committee said:
The waters of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago lie over the continental shelf; the Arctic islands and the continental shelf are a geological extension of the Canadian mainland and the North American land mass.
So, it seems to me on the basis of any one of the three doctrines, whether it is that of the sector claim, that of drawing the base lines from headland to headland, or on the basis of the continental shelf doctrine there seems to be an irrefutable case for Canada to claim complete sovereignty over the entire northern area from our mainland to the North Pole.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there are compelling reasons for Canada to assert its sovereignty, and for it to do so without any further delay.
First of all we must establish Canada's right to develop any petroleum or any other resources lying offshore from the Arctic islands. I think it is significant that the United States has never questioned Canadian sovereignty over these waters until recently. The only reason that our claims to sovereignty are being queried at this time is the oil discoveries in Prudhoe Bay, and from our point of view these discoveries have been followed by an even more important discovery of an oil well by the Imperial Oil Company in the Northwest Territories. These discoveries, along with other geological data which have been collected, give credence to the claim by many prominent geologists that the Arctic may well contain some of the largest oil reserves in the world.
Our failure to assert our jurisdiction at this time could mean that we might lose by default the right to develop vast resources which are so essential to the future development of Canada. The New Democratic party takes the position that Canada should clearly assert its right to its share of the Arctic continental shelf, and that we should get on with the task of discovering and developing the resources which are to be found there.
The second reason we ought to move, and move quickly on this matter, is that Canada must have jurisdiction over the northern 21611-32

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic waters in order to prevent disastrous and lingering pollution. As the committee pointed out, the sinking of two barges owned by Panarctic Oil Ltd. points up the danger of pollution in this area.
The Humble Oil Company of Texas, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of Standard Oil, has announced that it is studying the feasibility of constructing six 250,000 ton tankers, each of which would be twice the size of the Manhattan. Any mishap to a tanker of this size would have disastrous effects on the marine life of the Arctic. It will be noted in this morning's newspapers that over the past number of months some five super oil tankers have sunk in various parts of the world. Mr. Speaker, I contend that since Canada would be the main victim of any pollution which might occur from such a mishap, surely we ought to have the authority to exercise the necessary control to prevent such pollution from taking place.

Certainly, if we do not exercise it, nobody else is going to exercise control. There have been suggestions by prominent figures in the United States that Canada, instead of exercising pollution control on its own, should be prepared to delegate this responsibility to some international body, or through some international agreement. I think this would be disastrous, and I agree with the committee when it says, as printed at page 5 of its report:
Your committee is unimpressed with arguments that adequate pollution safeguards could be effected by international agreement.
Since it is Canadian terrain which would suffer the consequences of pollution I maintain that Canada has an inalienable right to exercise the necessary controls and to set the necessary standards which would hold pollution to a minimum.
The third reason I think we must move quickly is that only by the exercise of our sovereignty would Canada be able to facilitate and direct navigation in Arctic waters. These waters have never been part of the high seas and open to navigation. They are ice-locked for the major part of the year, and if they are used this can only be done with the navigational aids and the icebreaking services provided by the people of Canada. Needless to say this does not mean that we are suggesting that Canada should deny to any nation the right of innocent passage. On
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic the contrary, we feel that the Canadian government should proceed with all haste to provide the navigational aids, pilot services, navigation standards and the icebreaker escorts which will make possible innocent passage through Arctic waters. But there must be no doubt about who controls the navigation of these waters. By drawing baselines between the islands Canada can make the Arctic waters subject to Canadian legislative control, and that should be done immediately.

Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The
Islands): Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude by saying that in my opinion this is the time for Canada to make a clear and forthright declaration of its sovereignty over this great northern area.
The government's admission of uncertainty has been interpreted as weakness by our American neighbours. The government's diplomatic pussyfooting has merely demonstrated to other nations our lack of courage and conviction concerning Canada's claims to exclusive jurisdiction over the Arctic Archipelago and the continental shelf.
The Americans like straight talk and I think they would respect Canada for asserting its legitimate and long recognized rights in the Arctic. There is an old saying "Silence gives consent". If the government continues to waffle on this question, no one can blame the United States or any other nation for assuming that we are prepared to accept some compromise which would negate our ability to effectively control an area which is vital to the future development of this country.
The matter which the committee has brought to the attention of the House through its report is only one facet of a much larger problem, namely, Canada's diminishing control of its own affairs. The accelerating rate of takeovers by American corporations is eroding our economic independence. Attempts are being made to entice us into a continental energy policy which could well condemn us to be a nation of extraction industries, supplying raw materials and energy for the American industrial complex.
It is rather significant that the reports which came out of the meetings between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and secretary Walter Hickel in Washington suggested that part of the total energy policy would be some type of guarantee of the

Northwest Passage. We have not had any definitive statement from the minister on this question. If we are talking about merely allowing American ships to use that passageway, of course everyone would agree. But if it means some surrender of our sovereignty, some agreement to a bi-national control of that waterway, then we are giving up something which legitimately belongs to the people of this country, not only the present generation but for generations to come.
In addition to economic takeovers and in addition to a continental policy on energy integration, we are being queried on whether we have sovereignty over the Arctic waters at the very time when this area gives promise of being a veritable treasure house of resources.
The Canadian people are becoming increasingly concerned about the steady erosion of our sovereignty and the diminution of our economic independence. They are bewildered by the government's timidity and its continual waffling on matters which affect Canada's future as an independent, viable nation. I believe the decade upon which we have just embarked is crucial for Canada. I believe that we will emerge from the seventies either as a strong, united Canada with a potential for greatness or we will find ourselves absorbed as a junior partner in an American hegemony.
At the turn of this century a great Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, talked about the 20th century belonging to Canada. That vision has not as yet materialized but there are still 30 years to go, Mr. Speaker, so we still have time if we have the will, the courage and the energy we can make that vision come true and help Canada attain the destiny of which it is capable.
