Mr. Speaker, I want first to congratulate the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) for going ahead and putting the motion now before us.
Having not had the opportunity to go North with the committee on his study trip conducted at the time of the passage of the U.S. ship Manhattan, as I was sitting on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, I was surprised by the government's reluctance to accept the report that the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development submitted on his return and which was tabled on December 16 last.
I have perused this report and found nothing in it nor in its recommendations
21611-32^
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic which went against the present or future rights or needs of Canada in the Arctic Archipelago that we consider as being part of Canada. The members of this committee and apparently the opposition members and at least one Liberal member are all in agreement, which seems to indicate that the committee's recommendations are meeting with approval. In my view, the government should take it upon itself not only to accept these recommendations, but also to implement them.
Considering the recent developments that were preceded by the performance of the American ship Manhattan, we must make our position known today because it has become necessary to do so.
Several people are urging the Canadian government to take over the Arctic Islands, our northern shores and surrounding waters. The government should not however act in too great a hurry. Other countries, like Russia, have taken over neighbouring regions in a big rush. The development of Siberia had already begun by the time they realized they should have taken a closer look at it.
While the Canadian government should proclaim its sovereignty over the Arctic territories, however, it should not run the risk of committing some regrettable errors that would soon prove costly.
In my opinion, the Canadian government should assert its sovereignty on the Arctic for some reasons referred to in the committee report and also for others that are altogether worth studying.
In fact, we know that the Arctic islands are reproduction areas for some species of migratory birds which sometimes migrate as far as the United States. The American government as well as ours is keen on taking the necessary steps to prevent water pollution by ships inadequately fitted for Arctic navigation.
We also know that Arctic waters are breeding grounds for certain aquatic animals such as whales, seals, walruses, etc. This is why we must take certain preventive measures in order to avoid polluting Canadian waters. Scientists have reported that the icy waters of the Arctic are different from temperate waters or from the warmer waters of other oceans.
We know how difficult it was to fight the pollution caused by the oil tanker that went down near the coast of England, for instance, where waters are temperate. What would have happened if this incident had occurred
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic in the icy waters of the Arctic? We shall have to insist that people who will someday navigate these waters take all the necessary precautions.
The report of the committee, as can be seen in Votes and Proceedings, at page 209, include this recommendation, and I quote:
Your Committee recommends that:
A) Fanarctic Oils Limited should rely as much as possible on ice working cargo ships for supplies rather than entering the Arctic transportation business themselves, at least at this stage of its development. The discovery of oil in the Arctic Archipelago would call for a further reappraisal of Fanarctic's transportation role.
This committee recommendation must not apply to Panarctic Oils Limited only, but too any shipping company that would want to take to the Arctic materials required for the development of the natural wealth to be found there, or to carry back to the South the riches themselves.
There are still other reasons why Canada should claim sovereignty over the Arctic territories. As a matter of fact, those lands abound with natural wealth which we can develop and process ourselves.
I would now like to mention oil, iron and other natural resources even though up to the present time exploration has been rather limited considering the vast expanse of territory to develop. Nevertheless we And in those places considerable mineral deposits and oil fields.
For the above reasons we should proclaim our sovereignty over these territories by effective occupation. To this end, we must help the companies wishing to carry out prospec-tion in those areas. They must have all the necessary facilities for so doing.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
To achieve this end, I think we should give our coast guard the necessary authority, because the inspections they have been submitted to showed their efficiency particularly in the Arctic. Of all the countries in the world, Canada is probably the one that has the longest coastline. From inspections of our coast guard, we have been pleased to find out how efficient they are.
The government should also establish research and development centres on the Arctic islands. Our university graduates, our technicians and our engineers would be happy to make use of their knowledge for the benefit of their country. When the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence conducted an investigation last summer within the Navy and the Army, it was suggested,

and quite rightly, to set up guard stations that could be manned by members of the Canadian armed forces, in order to facilitate the movements of individuals in those regions.
Responsibilities should also be given to companies developing the natural resources of the Arctic, because it has unlimited wealth which should be worked.
It was said a few months ago that a mining consortium was interested in a ferrous deposit on Baffin Island containing, according to a preliminary study, 22 billion tons of 69 per cent pure iron ore. Apparently, such natural resources are to be found all over the Arctic islands and even on the neighbouring mainland.
Considering the development and research being carried out in all fields, water transportation for instance, it is obvious that if the government does not let opportunity knock in vain, the prospects are very good for the Canadian economy. I believe that it was the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) who mentioned a little while ago the developments that would probably take place in the transportation of oil and iron ore by cargo submarines.
An editorial in today's Le Devoir, a Montreal paper, reads as follows:
In a recent number of 1 'Actualite economique, there is an article by Mr. Michel Brochu about experiments carried out in Siberia. Placing a thin film of sand on the ice increases the action of the sun and makes the ice melt faster. Mr. Brochu believes that with the extended period of sunlight in northern regions during the summer, such a method, over several years, would permit the clearing of sea passages which could then be open to navigation each summer.
These experiments and research are being conducted now. It has not yet been possible to check whether they are conclusive, but we are continually being surprised by discoveries in all fields. I feel the government must immediately implement the recommendations of the committee whose report is before us today and take efficient though cautious steps in order to proclaim its sovereignty over the territories of northern Canada, and more specifically over the Arctic archipelago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention in the limited time I propose to take to deal with the subtleties and intricacies of international law with regard to the matter now before us, except to make some reference to the aspect which is of direct concern to me and for which I have some responsibility.
January 22, 1970

I refer to the conference on marine pollution held at Brussels in November of last year and which I attended as head of the Canadian delegation.
This matter is of considerable irrelevance to the subject we are discussing today because, in addition to the undoubted problems that have quite properly been raised during this debate with regard to pollution in the north, there is the fact that on a day to day basis, and on an almost immediate basis, we have a serious problem with regard to the waters around all of Canada.
It is my judgment, and I think I can support this by saying it is also the judgment of my department, that while we should not for a moment lose sight of the extremely important aspects of northern pollution, at the same time in terms of immediacy it is not as vitally important as what we do now with regard to all of the waters that surround Canada. I, therefore, do not think it is a deviation for me to touch briefly on some other matters regarding pollution for which I have a direct responsibility.
As some hon. members know, during the past week I had discussions with the United States authorities on questions such as jet pollution, the poisoning of our air by these new technological advances. We have also been very deeply engaged in studies on the amount of pollution that results from the emissions of automobiles. I am simply pointing out that while understandably the developments which I suggest were really triggered by the voyage of the S.S. Manhattan through the north are of supreme importance, nevertheless we ought not to consider these in isolation or be sidetracked in a sense to a total involvement on this particular question and this particular issue to the detriment of the kind of serious obligation that we ought to have on the whole pollution question.
With regard to the question of pollution of all marine environment, plus the air pollution as a result of the new type jet aircraft and as a result of automobile emissions, we are only starting to scratch the surface of what has become in these early days of the seventies probably the single most publicized subject. It is one which I think publicity reflects as being a real sense of concern not only to Canadians, but to people in many different parts of the world.
The totality of the effects of pollution is almost indescribable and in fact almost unbelievable. I came across some figures today which, although perhaps not completely relevant to the subject under discussion, may
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic be of interest to hon. members. I ask Your Honour's indulgence for 60 seconds. These figures reveal that in terms of garbage, 250 indestructible bottles are abandoned every year by each person in the country, 135 tin cans, 10 gallons of sewage per day per person and 4 pounds of solid sewage wastes per day per person. A lot of this garbage is going into our modern environment. These items are direct contributors to pollution and I repeat the totality of these in some respects is a more serious and more immediate problem than the potentialities of pollution in our northern areas.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In effect, then, even given the greatest possible technological advances and even if the decision were made to employ ships for the transport of oil through northern waters it appears now it would be some time, perhaps years, before this could be accomplished.
We in Canada learnt a good deal from the so-called Manhattan experiment. Hon. members will, I am sure, agree with me that our coastguard demonstrated a world wide level of expertise in the work it did during that venture. I think it is safe to say that when it comes to any kind of navigation through ice and the like there is no country, with the possible exception of the Soviet Union, which could carry on such activities without Canada's assistance. I mention this, apart from the natural pride I have as the minister responsible for the coastguard, by way of reiterating my comment that while I do not minimize the gravity of this threat the more serious danger at the moment is, rather, that which might result from the huge tankers which are in operation right now. For example, Halifax in recent months has been visited by tankers having a capacity larger than that of the Torrey Canyon. At any moment of time, there are hundreds of tankers along our coasts, and it is because of this threat that we took the very hard line we did at the Brussels conference.
In this connection, in response to some of the comments which have been made about the wisdom and effectiveness of taking unilateral action, let me say there is no question that this is a strongly emotional and appealing approach. It is one which commends itself to people who wish merely to put something on record or to put something in the window. Having gone through the Brussels experience and seen, in terms of international affairs, the enormous number of conflicting viewpoints which are expressed on many of these issues,
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic I have had personal experience at least in learning how difficult it is to secure international agreement and also how futile it is in many ways to take a strong, unilateral stance in the face of overwhelming opposition from other countries.
At the Brussels conference it was our intention to move for an international agreement concerning responsibility for the prevention of oil pollution and the establishment of standard international rules with regard to carriers and the like. In the second place, we wished to define clearly where responsibility lay when one of these spills occurred on the high seas. Initially, back in June, I think, of last year, we introduced into the Canada Shipping Act a number of amendments, one of which was designed to pinpoint this responsibility more specifically than in the past. However, since the Brussels conference was opening at that time it was agreed, with the approval of opposition parties, that we would not press for the enactment of this particular amendment in the House because we wanted to wait to see what happened as a result of the international discussions. Since my return I have been awaiting a report from the delegates who represented Canada throughout the meetings in Brussels. I had undertaken to make a statement on motions in the House in connection with the outcome at that conference, but it seems to me that in view of the arrangements made for today's debate this might be an appropriate point to report on exactly what did transpire. In addition, I thought I might give some indication of what we propose to do.
The Canadian position at this conference was squarely grounded upon two aspects of our experience. For many years the Navigable Waters Protection Act has provided for the removal of wrecks interfering with navigation at the expense of the owner without limitation of liability or the requirement to prove fault. Responsibility for the removal of wrecks lay with the owners. Significant pollution incidents had occurred on our coasts even before the loss of the Torrey Canyon, and preventive measures were taken at the expense of the government in the absence of legislation providing for recovery. An amendment to the Canada Shipping Act proposed to Parliament early last year which would have gone some way to meeting this problem was, as I have explained, held over in the hope that the Brussels conference would provide adequately for such a contingency on an international basis.
IMr. Jamieson.]
Our stance at the conference, arising naturally from our own experience, had two principal policy objectives. The first was that the commercial movement of noxious cargoes, particularly oil, should in no way impose burdens upon innocent third parties or the states of which those parties are citizens. The second was that each form of transportation, should, so far as is feasible, bear its own costs-a principle laid down in the National Transportation Act. The government believes this principle to be necessary for the efficient use of our collective resources. In other words, what we asserted was that in the event of a spill on the high seas which affected the Canadian coastline in any way there should be no responsibility placed upon the aggrieved party, either the nation of Canada or some private person, as a result of something which was clearly no part of their responsibility.
Against this background, the conventions produced by the conference fell far short of what Canada considers to be satisfactory, particularly as to liability for pollution damage. We found it almost totally impossible to achieve any degree of unanimity among the countries concerned, and for a variety of reasons in which hon. members may be interested. For one thing, a great many of the oil producing countries possess very little coastline. Others have large shipping companies in which they are specially interested even though they may possess a certain amount of coastline. So there is no unanimity of concern, and, basically, most countries react subjectively in these matters.
However, the Canadian delegation gained the distinct impression that many of the delegations to this legal conference went there with the prime purpose merely of obtaining a determination of the legal and financial position of ship owners in the event of further incidents of the Torrey Canyon type. There is evidence that a nation which is a very important shipping nation has this as its primary concern, often because its coastline is decidedly limited, or, indeed-though this may at first appear somewhat curious-it may not have a coastline at all.
In these circumstances the Canadian delegation seems to have made some impact. I do not wish to exaggerate, but I feel we have made an impact which improves our situation and which may well do so in fuller measure in the future. This is because, as a coastal state with a limited merchant fleet, our attention was focussed on the substantive conse-
January 22, 1970

quences of a major oil spill rather than on the legal rights of one of the parties. We were able to make the case strongly that in any such incident which might occur along our coastline we would likely be the sufferer, without any continuing advantages, because we are neither a large merchant marine owning country nor are we an exporting country to any large extent in terms of the use of tankers.
Among other things, the conventions declare the right of a coastal state to intervene on the high seas, place a requirement for proof of absence of fault upon the shipowner, nearly double the traditional amount of the limitation of liability for the shipowner and provide for compulsory insurance so that bankruptcy cannot be used to avoid payment.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Many of these points were included as a result of the urging of Canadian delegates, both at the prior committee work and at the conference itself. Since this is a rather complex subject I do not wish to labour it before the House but I will be pleased to provide a copy of this statement to interested members.
Even more important, the Canadian attitude at this conference encouraged the Belgian government to put forward a proposal and the conference to endorse a study of the establishment of an international fund, financed by a levy on oil cargos moved by sea, which would compensate victims of pollution before not covered by ship owner's strict liability. A conference is to be held in 1971 to consider the results of this study with a view to a further convention, which the House will note relates to liability to be placed on the cargo owner as advocated by Canada in addition to the limited liability of the ship owner. At the present time almost universally it is the ship owner who bears the brunt of the responsibility, such as it is, and the owner of the cargo being transported in that vessel, unless it happens to be one and the same organization, is more or less absolved of any responsibility. We think this is an improper situation primarily. In addition, it is not always possible for the ship owner to get the kind of insurance or related protection we feel is necessary if these massive spills and their effects are to be avoided.
We understand that some other governments are now contemplating national funds of this sort. Others are considering alternative means of achieving similar ends. I may say in terms of the Canadian position that we are

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic now looking at the possibility of levying some form of assessment against vessels moving within Canadian waters to establish this type of fund against possible future spills because we think this will help in part to resolve the situation. I think we may expect increasing support from such countries which may now be considering the broader implications of this question.
Against this background, the government of Canada is now giving active consideration to interim measures in light of the Brussels conference. Clearly, we did not achieve what we had set out to achieve. It may be that we were too ambitious in the first instance or perhaps especially conscious and realistic enough to realize in advance that we were looking for more than we would achieve. In any event, we made the position very strongly as I have outlined to you here today. As a result, I believe there was more in the way of endorsation of our position than there might have been had we not taken this firm, and what some regard as extreme, stand. In any event, we are now examining possible interim measures.
This is, of course, part of the larger and more general question of pollution, including that from noxious substances other than oil and, pollution of coastal waters from sources other than ships. This, too, has become an increasing problem within the context of the outline at the beginning of my remarks concerning the totality of the pollution problem. There is the matter of oil drilling with rigs, and there are all manner of other sources which are now pumping potential pollution into our coastal waters. So, again it is not just a simple matter of saying if we cut off these sources of pollution at one particular point we can breathe easily. If I could mix a metaphor a little bit, perhaps we will not be able to breathe at all, unless we approach the whole subject and try to deal with it in some decisive manner. This is part of the over-all picture.
The proposals now being developed in respect of pollution from ships have as their objective the attainment of our goals at the conference to the extent that this is possible by one country acting alone. In other words, what we have said is, since we have not been able to achieve international agreement at this time on the question of how to control this type of pollution, we will take the same goals and set them as our objectives, then ask ourselves the question; acting unilaterally what can we do? Once we have arrived at
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic those answers, then my intention is to introduce further amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. I am sure they will receive rapid response and endorsement by members on all sides.
At the same time, we will continue by seeking to ensure that our actions in respect of the various aspects of this total problem will conform to a consistent pattern. Interdepartmental discussions are now going forward with this objective in mind. As soon as these discussions and considerations can be concluded, I will be bringing forward proposed amendments and appropriate legislation.
I know this is a rather frustrating kind of position because what it really admits is that spilling can take place and there is always the danger that, in spite of everything we do, we will have a disaster of the magnitude of the Torrey Canyon incident or one even worse. We have to think about this when members are referring to the north and the potential problem there, and I put that word in quotation marks because we do have a particular reason in some areas to anticipate some of these things.
A potential problem in the north, however far removed it might be, taken against the real problem for example within the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the St. Lawrence seaway or at some point in our inland waters, is important. So, in addition to thinking about pollution and how to correct it to the best of our ability after it happens, equally as important-one might be prepared to agree that it is more important-is to put in the most stringent regulations possible so that these spills will not take place. This will involve standards for vessels that carry oil and our ability to ensure that vessels that do not meet these standards do not enter these waters over which we have control.
This again is a rather difficult problem but one with which we are coping through design standards and specifications. There is an international question here as to just how far, even with the new conventions to which I referred as agreed to in Brussels, we can go in terms of moving out into the high seas. Certainly, we would not be entitled in terms of inspecting a hull to determine whether it was adequate to meet our standards. There is also the question of navigable waters and a lot of other things to which carriers do not agree.
Perhaps the most pressing of all in many respects, because this is the insidious part of the problem, are the relatively small spills

that take place either as the result of carelessness or "I don't give a damn" attitude on the part of certain carriers. In the last year we have stepped up our inspection activities considerably throughout those areas of our waters where it is possible for us to do so.
What I have touched upon is only a small part of the story, but I thought it might be helpful in light of this present discussion for hon. members to know something about what has transpired; first of all the position that Canada took, which is still our stand in this regard, and secondly how extremely difficult it is because of the variety of things involved to achieve international agreement on a question of this kind. In addition, to repeat what I said earlier, it is difficult when one takes unilateral action to be in a position to impose regulations in any meaningful way.
I do not believe in repeating something I said at the beginning, but simply having something in the window is not of very much consequence unless you have the means, the authority and the power, if you like, to enforce any regulations you might decide to impose unilaterally. But I believe many of these things are within our competence, and whenever it is, members of this House can be assured we will move ahead with the measures I have outlined today which I hope will take legislative form before too long. This will move us ahead significantly in what is a most crucial battle against this present day threat of pollution.

It seems to me there is a serious reluctance to concur in the report of the committee which is the substance of this motion. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) for having moved the motion. I wish also to congratulate the hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) who, although he criticized me somewhat in the process, had the courage to take a strong position on the side of what he considered to be the right position, the concurrence in this report and the adoption by the government of the position taken by the committee in this report. I congratulate the hon. gentlemen.
The board chairman of the Humble Oil Company, a company frequently referred to in the course of this debate, in briefing the news media on the Arctic voyage of the Manhattan welcomed the gentlemen of the press to the world's largest and most expensive edition of the Ice Follies. He may stand to be corrected as to whether it will prove to be the largest and most expensive edition of the Ice Follies. He may stand to be corrected if this government does not indicate to the world without delay that vessels, surface and submarine, passing through Canada's Arctic Archipelago are and shall be subject to the sovereign control and regulation of Canada.
This, of course, is the view so eloquently expressed by the committee in its report. The committee made this recommendation after considering the potential threat of maritime oil tanker traffic through the waters of the Archipelago and the threat to Canada's environment in the north. Members of the committee had an opportunity for discussion with experts in the oil industry, with our own icebreaker marine officials, and with leading

DEBATES	January 22, 1970
Canadian marine biologists and ecologists investigating the sinking last August of the two Panarctic barges off Melville Island. The committee states:
However, your Committee shares the concern of most Canadians and of conservationists throughout the world of the dangers of pollution inherent in any future oil tanker maritime traffic through Canada's Arctic waters. Your Committee is convinced that the safeguards and pollution controls necessary to protect Canada's Arctic environment and ecology will neither be possible nor enforceable without an effective exercise of Canadian control over the waters and the ships using the waters of Canada's Arctic Archipelago.
That quotation is the heart of the recommendation of the committee and goes to the very core of the debate we are having here today. Following that, the committee further states:
Your Committee is unimpressed with arguments that adequate pollution safeguards could be effected by international agreement.
Of course, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) certainly said nothing here today which would lead us to believe there is any immediate prospect of international accords to prevent the disaster happening which we are afraid might happen. It may very well be, and I assume it is, that the Minister of Transport had business to which he must attend following the termination of his speech, but even if I had nothing to do after making a speech in such an irrelevant way I, too, would have left the House very quickly.

Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much whether by 1975 we will have the answers to the ecological problems raised by these probes into the north. Certainly, there will be a real threat to our environment. Surely, in these circumstances we must assert our sovereignty. Of course, we must ourselves pioneer this area to see how best it can be used for the benefit of the Canadian people, more particularly of the native people who stand to lose all by an unfettered outside exploitation of their homeland.
Secondly, we must maintain firm control over the environment, not just for ourselves but in a very real sense for the whole world. I do not wish to exaggerate, but it may very well be that here our whole future lies in the balance, and that a wrong movement by the government, or the failure to make the right move merely to satisfy the economic interests of our neighbours to the south, or some timidity on the subject, may well contribute to the environmental breakdown of the world. Certainly, this is what many fear.
I say, Sir, that we have the political power to assert sovereignty, but what the government needs is the will to assert sovereignty. What we need today is a little bit of the guts that went into the making of Canada in the first place.

It is time we acted effectively, and if we don't we may be welcoming what will be, in fact, the world's largest and most expensive edition of the Ice Follies, and the chairman of Humble Oil may prove to have been wrong.
I welcome, in a sense, the information given us by the Minister of Transport with regard to international discussions and the tentative steps taken toward the achievement of some international agreement respecting pollution in international waters. That is a sort of side-effect to this debate. We have been trying to get a statement from the minister about what went on at that conference ever since it was held, but it took a motion such as this one and an effort to try to distract the attention of the House and of the country from the essential point in this discussion get this statement from the minister. Anyway, we are happy to have it and I think we still have plenty of time to discuss the relevant matters.
I repeat that that statement has nothing to do with the case at all.
May I just draw the attention of the House to the fact that, even if there were any prospect that such an international agreement could be achieved in the immediate future, it would not be sufficient. The minister spoke about the sanctions. He spoke about firms and perhaps countries being required to make deposits so that those who suffered financially would be reimbursed. But, Mr. Speaker, financial reimbursement is not going to meet this problem in the north. This problem is not something you can fix up with money, short of enormous expenditures which would only go part way.
What we are so concerned about is the possibility of irreparable injury being done that cannot be compensated by money. So, Mr. Speaker, what the minister was talking about was completely irrelevant; first of all because it applies to international waters; secondly, because it shows no prospect of coming about in the near future; and, thirdly, because in any event it would be inadequate even if it came into effect in the very near future.

On October 24 last the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of Canada told this House:
First of all, we will never sacrifice, in the name of progress, a clean and healthy environment to industrial or commercial development.
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
The only way that the government of Canada can prevent the sacrifice of the north, can prevent the sacrifice of this clean and healthy environment, is by claiming the power to exercise, and by exercising, effective control. Nobody else is going to exercise that control.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are various recommendations in the committee's report. The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) referred to them. He suggested that the adoption of the report might force the government to take measures involving the expenditure of public money. But surely, Sir, that is not so. Surely, that is another red herring. I say quite frankly that that has nothing to do with the case.
If the House adopts this motion, as I hope it will, the government is not committed to the expenditure of a cent, but it does express to the government the unanimous views of the members of the House. I do not imagine, Mr. Speaker, that the government will pay very much more attention to the views of the House as a whole than it does to the views of the Opposition as a whole. But in any event, it is not right to suggest that it is a poor pract ce to move this kind of a motion because it may involve the government in the expenditure of money. That is not so. It is perfectly proper for the House to adopt this motion expressing its view on the desirability of the government doing something, the desirability of it adopting some policies. That is what is being done here. The House is being asked to recommend to the government of Canada the adoption of certain policies.
What possible reason could there be for the government refusing to declare Canada's sovereignty over the north? What possible reason is there for the government refusing to carry out the basic recommendation of this committee? Any adequate reason has certainly not been disclosed. Certainly, I have not heard it. Evidently the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin has not heard it. None of us heard it.
There are obvious reasons why it is important that the government should move. Every day of silence on the part of the government increases the conviction of other countries about the doubts Canada may have of the validity of her claims. I think there can be no doubt about that. Secondly, every day that goes by increases the possibility that dangers and difficulties may arise for which we are not prepared, so it is urgent, sir, that we move. This resolution is not going to put the

cabinet in a straitjacket, but it will indicate very clearly to the government of this country what members of this House feel on a matter that is essential to the future of our country. There is real urgency in view of the possibility of pollution, but there are longer term factors indicating the importance of Canada's claiming sovereignty over the waters between the Archipelago and the mainland of Canada. This is surely essential to the development of the north; it is not a matter of making this claim through any sense of imperialism. It is necessary to make it for ensuring the development of the nation.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The report refers to fishing. We cannot see at this time what the resources in the northern waters may be; we cannot see at this time who may wish to exploit these with the techniques that may be available in the future. It is essential for the protection of Canadian interests and the realization of Canada's destiny in the north, that the government stop fooling around and take the necessary position.
There has been a fair amount of discussion about precedents and a fair amount of discussion about innocent passage. I could go into all that, but I think the position is pretty clear and I will not worry the House with too many legal discussions. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, first of all, given that Canada has undisputed claims both to the Arctic Archipelago and the continental shelf extending from its northern shores, and that Canada has by exploration and other activities shown a concern for the polar area to the north, that we should declare our interests in that whole polar sector. This would not be done through any sense of imperialism or aggression but because Canada believed that its national interest must be protected from the devastating results that unrestricted activities in the area may produce.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we must be alert to the dangers that may arise outside our territorial waters to the north. We must be alert to the colossal calamities that may take place within that polar sector and we must be prepared to take action. This is not only necessary in our own interests but I believe we have a duty to take such action if we are to discharge our duties to Canada today and in the future and, indeed, to the world. At the present time nobody else is going to worry very much about disasters that may take place in these waters.
January 22, 1970

In addition to this, the least we should do in accordance with existing legislative policy is draw base lines around the whole of the Arctic Archipelago, reducing the intervening waters to the status of internal waters. I take this to be the substance of the recommendation of the committee, notwithstanding the fact that some of the straits are twice the width of the Canadian territorial waters.
I suggest without hesitation that this is justifiable under international law on the grounds which have been referred to today and expounded in the Norwegian Fisheries question and the Convention on the Territorial Seas, and also having regard to the special nature of the waters concerned. In doing so, Canada does not deny that there might be a right of innocent passage through the Northwest Passage but we must, and again not for the purpose of asserting our rights but in order to discharge our responsibilities, assert that any claims to innocent passage or right to innocent passage is contingent upon the approval of Canadian authorities.

This is justifiable and legal for the following reasons. First of all, there is no customary international trade route through the Northwest Passage, unless there is a customary right of innocent passage, which certainly does not apply.
Secondly, it is in the interest of Canadian security to protect the resources of the area and to restrict certain categories of vessel, particularly tankers, from using it unless they can meet the standards set by Canada.
Thirdly, in view of the large investment, it will be necessary to provide navigational and meteorological aids, icebreakers, charting services, safety and rescue equipment. It may very well be necessary to levy charges for these services on vessels using the Northwest Passage.
Fourthly, in view of all this, the Northwest Passage possesses many of the features of an internal waterway, a fact which imposes severe limitations on the right of innocent passage.
I think members in all parts of the House must be very puzzled as to what is wrong with the government. What is really standing in the way of the government taking action which I think we are all convinced is necessary for the welfare of our country? Certainly, it is dangerous for the government not to do so, confusion thus being created and risks run.

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic Certainly, if there are valid reasons, the government is keeping them very secret.

Nobody denies it. The government does not deny sovereignty. The government says there is no necessity as yet to put our foot down and say we are the king of this little castle. As hon. members opposite have said, it is recognized that the archipelago, the islands in the north, are Canadian territory. Who is questioning this? Why do we have to say at this time that we are the sovereign rulers of this land and of this channel? What we are really concerned about is the danger of pollution.
Why do hon. gentlemen think the United States are less concerned about this matter than we are? Surely no one would suggest that the United States would be glad to have this channel recognized as international water. They certainly would not want to see Russian or Chinese ships in this channel. We have explained our position. We have received consideration from the United States government and the corporations that are developing the oil reserves. I am sure we can come to some agreement.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) pointed out, it does not have to be an international agreement, because other nations are not concerned; they do not care. The Minister of Transport admitted at the Brussels conference there was not much likelihood of an international agreement. But
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic why do we need an international agreement? Why can we not have a dialogue with the other country concerned, the United States? Surely we can come to a rational agreement whereby the United States will recognize our problems and our apprehensions, and will come to an agreement if necessary whereby a fee can be charged and we will have some insurance against pollution caused by oil spillage.
I have no doubt that the United States would also agree that Canada should have a much stronger voice, and possibly the majority voice, in the administration of regulations and the surveillance of the construction of ships to ensure that there is less likelihood of danger. It seems hon. members opposite are not expressing their apprehension as to the danger involved but want to make absolutely sure there will never be any spillage. This is impossible.
If Canadians want the north to be opened, we cannot say that we want the passage to be opened at absolutely no risk to ourselves. We have to take some risk. We have to ensure that if ships, are allowed to go through, we have the final say as to their construction, not necessarily unilaterally but we should have a strong voice in indicating the type of ships we will approve and the type of navigation we will accept to at least protect ourselves from the possible dangers of pollution.
Until now we have been speaking entirely of oil pollution, but there is nothing to guarantee that at a later time nations which have a problem in disposing of nuclear garbage will have to transport it great distances. That in itself would create a problem. All these problems are unforeseen now, but we cannot say we will not allow anyone to go through this passage unless we are absolutely sure there is no danger. This is nonsense. We cannot do it. We must say that we want the north to be opened up and that we want development there.
The Canadian government has a great interest in the Panarctic and we expect to have more. United States businessmen have put over $800 million into part of their territory in order to explore it and obtain oil. They also have responsibility as well as rights. Why do we have to concern them and the world by saying, "This is our territory. We are the sovereign power and you cannot do anything unless you ask us and abide by our terms"?

The Canadian government failed to obtain international agreement at the Brussels conference I think they should get together with the only other nation concerned and reach agreement as quickly as possible to control

this pollution and to And ways and means of obtaining money, whether by fees, tolls or otherwise, to research the problem and lay down the law. Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned at six o'clock I was saying that the matter under discussion is extremely urgent if we want to ensure the security, welfare and future of the Canadian population.
But it seems that our ever so wise government wishes to ignore the report tabled in the House. It is rather strange that the government should disregard the report of one of its committees in view of the ever increasing importance of the functions of the committees since parliamentary reforms were enacted. This can only be explained by the fact that the conclusions of the committee are in direct conflict with the government policy in regard to Canadian Arctic waters.
And if, by chance, the government should, with the help of its majority or some contrivance, determine tonight to give this report a first class funeral, this would mean that it does not trust the work of the committees and that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talked about parliamentary reforms, it was simply a smoke screen.
Should the government decide tonight, owing to its majority, not to implement the recommendations of the committee, there would be only one thing left for the members of the committee to do, and this, in order to protect the rights and privileges of all hon. members who sit on committees of the House: all of them should, in one gesture of solidarity, resign from the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Thus they would prove to the people that the

government disregards the committee reports which are submitted to its attention.
I was saying at the beginning of my remarks that we are living a historic moment, because the House, pursuant to the Chair's ruling, has set a precedent. The government rarely takes objection in the House to the presentation of a committee report. Should it persist in refusing the reports presented by committees, it will be severely judged when the time comes by public opinion.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
By refusing to assert Canada's sovereignty over the Arctic waters, the government shows clearly that he understands neither the importance of the interests at stake nor the seriousness of the situation.
The government believes that by negotiating an international agreement against pollution, it will assert our sovereignty. Far from asserting our sovereignty, such ac'.ion will not even succeed in protecting Canada from water pollution in this area. Such a position is particularly illogical and dangerous because how can we enforce an agreement concerning an area which we are not even sure to possess? Any protective measure against pollution is impossible and inapplicable if Canada does not exercise effective control over the waters of the Canadian archipelago and over the ships that will use them. The need for a declaration of sovereignty does not arise from the simple fact of a recommendation to this effect by the committee.
The immediate declaration by the government of the Canadian sovereignty over the waters of the continental shelf is called for the following reasons: first, in order to be effective, any international agreement aimed at removing the danger of pollution in the Arctic waters demands, first, a declaration of sovereignty. The simple fact that some countries are already studying the use of the Northwest Passage for commercial transportation and that large companies are carrying out their activities in these regions should encourage the government to state right now and unequivocally its sovereignty over this region.
Canada cannot afford to wait for universal consensus since two ships of the Panarctic Oils Limited, one of which was carrying oil, have already gone down in this area.
We must first of all realize that there is no danger of pollution in the Arctic waters. Much is at stake for Canada, for the Arctic waters are a hunting ground for Indians and Eskimos, 8,500 to 10,500 of them respectively.
January 22, 1970

Humanitarian and economic considerations are therefore involved.
Does the government refuse to proclaim our sovereignty in the Arctic for fear of certain legal consequences?
Obviously, if Canada allows other countries to move in-I now refer to the international aspect-it may be far more difficult in the future to prove our sovereignty before the competent tribunal. But if the government took concrete steps immediately, and moved into the field we already hold, it might be easier to refute the claims of other countries, including the United States and to refute legal arguments before the international Court.
I still wonder why the government is reluctant to make that statement; I suspect they may fear its legal consequences.
If they really want to test that sovereignty, let them do it now and let the countries that want to dispute it make out their case before the International Court of Justice.
One must realize first of all that much of the natural resources in the Arctic waters are only partially developed and that they are priceless. It is a must for Canada to establish effectively, for future generations, her sovereignty as well as navigation security in that area.
As desirable as international control of water pollution could be, it is but one of the consequences of a statement on sovereignty, as I said a while ago. The delicate ecological balance in the Arctic must be preserved, for the sake of its population and its animal life.
The Manhattan's journey through the Northwest Passage has opened a new era. The economic development of that area, the oil and ore resources of its maritime subsoil and their development depend first of all upon a vigorous statement of sovereignty if Canada wants to remain in the race. This country cannot afford to jeopardize the future of her citizens, her animal and plant life and her natural resources.
The Canadian people have a right to expect efficient measures from the government, for their future is at stake. A firm and clear statement of the Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic waters is the first step to take before formulating a policy on Arctic waters.
Such a statement on sovereignty should obviously be tied in with the passage of several pieces of legislation not only to uphold the occupation of Arctic territories but also to state precisely the legal question as to that very important problem.

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
The need for a statement on sovereignty, as I said a while ago, is also urgent. Indeed, the fragile ecological balance of the Arctic is already threatened. On Melville Island, where Panarctic Oils Limited is conducting explorations, there are thousands of empty oil drums scattered about the island. The delicate wildlife of the island has already fallen a victim to the machinery in use there.
This is only the first problem, for Canada will certainly very soon discover oil and other minerals. As we know, companies are busy exploring in this area.
The government should realize that pollution is only one of the problems that should induce it to solve, right away and for all the world to know, the problem of sovereignty.
In its eagerness to have the people take part in the administration of the country, the government is gradually leading us to believe that the country is run by rumours coming from everywhere.
Concerning this important question, there have been rumours abroad to the effect that Canada had established strict control in the area of the Arctic waters, but these were just pompous statements of policy; no positive steps were ever taken.
Canadians are beginning to wonder seriously about the failure of this government to assume its responsibilities when it comes to firmly asserting the sovereignty of our country over its national heritage.
We know there are, in this area, many resources which need to be protected-and here I am talking to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp)-even if we have to exchange with the United States some strong and straight forward arguments about what we believe to be our sovereignty over this area of the country.
I think that the Canadian government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are mature enough to formulate themselves the foreign and domestic policy of Canada without having them being dictated by Washington.
If this problem is set out in clear and specific terms, the Washington government will be able to understand our position and it will be the first to recognize that we have taken a concrete and strong action which will be respected not only by our neighbours to the South but also by all the other countries which get some benefit out of their presence in that area.

We know that the Canadian people are greatly concerned about this problem. I would also submit that Quebecers do not remain indifferent to the harmful effects that the pollution of the Ungava and New Quebec areas would have.
We are entitled to know the opinion of the government in that respect and I hope that tonight the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs will make it known to us. The only way to deal with the matter would be for a member of the government or the Prime Minister himself to make a clear and precise statement with regard to our sovereignty over the Arctic waters. Should the Prime Minister refuse to abide by the wish of the committee and of most hon. members in that respect, he would indicate by his action that he leads a monolithic government which has no consideration for the opinion of the majority of hon. members.

I will deal with this point presently. The hon. member has put his finger exactly on the point at issue here. The report is a very good example of the way in which committees can be used to contribute to public understanding and to the understanding of this House on matters of such difficulty and complexity. However, under our parliamentary system of responsible government it is not the function of committees to usurp the responsibilities of government.
While it is true that the report of the committee is only a recommendation to the government to take certain action, and concurrence of the House cannot change its essential nature, to ask the House to concur in a report which makes so many specific recommendations requires the members of the government who are members of the House, if they take their responsibilities seriously-as I hope we all do-to express the points upon which they may differ from the committee even if they find the general tenor of the report to be valuable and acceptable.
To vote against the report could, on the other hand, be interpreted as a vote against the principle of Canada's sovereignty over the waters lying between the islands of the Canadian Archipelago. While the government may be generally sympathetic to the views of the committee, it may in the exercise of its responsibilities believe that it is necessary to adopt a strategy different from that advocated by the committee in order to attain the agreed objectives. I think the House will agree that this is understandable.
The committee does not have the responsibility of government. It does not have to weigh one objective or one priority against
January 22, 1970

another. The committee cannot answer tor the consequences of its own recommendations. On the other hand, the government must answer for the consequences of all its policies and all its actions. It cannot blame a committee, even if it accepts its findings, for mistakes which may result from the acceptance of the committee's report. I can assure the House that the recommendations of the committee will be given the most careful consideration by the government in framing the legislation to be proposed to Parliament.
What the government has been doing goes further than the approach suggested in the committee's report. We have not hesitated or delayed in determining our basic objectives, or in announcing them to the House and indeed to the world. These objectives were stated in the Speech from the Throne and in the Prime Minister's address in the Throne Speech debate. They are to encourage the development of Arctic navigation and to ensure the preservation of the Arctic environment. I am certain there is agreement on all sides with these objectives.
To translate them into practical terms, however, and to incorporate them into detailed legislation requires time and much study. We have taken our time and we have given the most careful thought to the process of implementing the basic policy which we have already stated, because the interests involved are of the greatest importance to the country. Mr. Speaker, the government has almost finished its work and we will be submitting the results to the House in the near future.
There is, I believe, no fundamental difference between the views of the government and of the committee as to the extent of Canada's sovereignty in the Arctic region. There is certainly no difference of view as to the necessity of taking action to control pollution. How best to reinforce Canadas' claims to sovereignty, and how best to use that authority to control pollution are problems of a different order. It is not sufficient, for this purpose, simply to make declarations and lay claims. I am sure those members of the House who are much more learned in the law than I will agree with this. This is a practice they follow in their own profession. These declarations may be challenged; these claims may be resisted. It becomes then of the utmost importance to proceed in such a way as to maximize the chances of acceptability and success. As in so many other fields, timing is of the essence.
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said on October 24 of last year:
There is not now, nor is it conceivable that there will ever be from any source, challenges to Canadian sovereignty on the mainland, in the islands, in the minerals lying in the continental shelf below the Arctic waters, or in our territorial seas. This happy situation is the result of quiet, consistent policies on the part of all Canadian governments. The present government pledges to be equally consistent. Those policies will reflect Canada's proper interest not only in the preservation of the ecological balance . . . but as well in the economic development of the north, the security of Canada, and in our stature and reputation in the world community.
To judge from some articles in the press and from various statements and speeches one would almost be led to believe that the Manhattan discovered the New World with the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria, This, of course, is not the case.
Canada was present and active in the Arctic and the Arctic waters for a century and more before the voyage of the Manhattan. The Manhattan project would not have been possible without the preparatory work, the scientific research, the investments, and the pioneering activities which successive Canadian governments have encouraged or undertaken over a vast area of the north. I refer to the systematic mapping, the hydrographic charting, the geophysical exploration and the sea-ice studies carried out by this country. Canada is not a newcomer to Arctic navigation. Canadian skills go away back and were demonstrated in historic voyages of the St. Roch and the Labrador. They were demonstrated again last fall when the John A. Macdonald escorted the Manhattan through Canada's northern islands and repeatedly freed her from the ice.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We are not unprepared for developments such as the Prudhoe Bay oil discoveries, the exploitation of Canada's own offshore Arctic resources and the commercial navigation of the Northwest Passage which may follow. We are ready for the opening of the Canadian Arctic for development, and that development is one of our great national objectives. It is with this in mind that we have stressed the desirability of keeping the Arctic waters open for innocent passage. We will do what is necessary for this purpose.
At the same time, however, we have also recognized that the danger of pollution by ships in the Arctic is particularly grave. Ice is the chief obstacle in these waters, but other
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic Arctic features are also a great hindrance, such as the extreme cold, the almost continuous fog and overcast, the 24-hour darkness in winter, the magnetic disturbances and deviations, the absence of distinctive landmarks and the need for extensive aids to navigation. Not only is there a high risk of accident, but the pollution damage resulting from an accident involving a supertanker could have a catastrophic effect upon the fragile ecology of the Arctic because of the slow workings of the biological processes which in more temperate areas effect a natural cleansing and healing operation. We do not know enough about some of these problems, but we are keenly aware of the potential dangers and we are determined to do what is necessary to minimize and avoid them.
Much has been said in this debate about international law with reference to the Arctic waters. The Prime Minister and I have both had something to say on this question on a number of occasions and I will not repeat all our previous observations here. I only wish to reaffirm a few points. The law of the sea is indeed a complex subject involving political, economic and security interests which are both national and international in scope.
This body of law has changed a great deal over the centuries with the growth of technology and shifts in the relations between states. It has undergone particularly rapid change in recent years, and Canada has made some contribution to its development to our national advantage. The Arctic seas represent a spec al situation which has so far received insufficient attention. There are obvious differences between ordinary water and water in its frozen state. Men can walk on the ice. Some people I am told can walk on the water, but generally speaking they can walk on the ice; they can shoot polar bears on the ice; they can commit murder on the ice. We all know that the flag state has jurisdiction over a crime committed on board a ship 60 miles from shore. But who has jurisdiction over a crime committed on the ice 60 miles from shore? The Canadian courts have provided effective answers to this question without feeling a need to refer to some stirring manifesto.
With respect to the Northwest Passage, one thing seems clear. As I wrote last September in an article in the Toronto Globe and Mail:
Heretofore, no one, be he Arctic expert, international jurist or government spokesman, could allege that the Northwest Passage is already an international strait under international law. If that were the case, we would not require now the

massive effort which we are witnessing for the purpose of forcing one ship and two icebreakers through the passage. In other words, we are not talking about established sea lanes or straits. We are talking about an area covered by solid ice through most of the year in some places and all of the year in others.
One last and most important point with respect to international law is this: I have already emphasized the importance the government attaches to keeping the Arctic waters open for innocent passage. We do not believe that the passage of ships which threaten the destruction or deterioration of the coastal environment can be considered innocent under any interpretation of international law. We have made clear to the world that while Canada welcomes the use of the Arctic waters as a transportation route for the vessels of all flags, the Canadian government will ensure that these waters are used for peaceful purposes and by ships complying with required safety standards.
In his statement of October 24 on the Throne Speech debate, the Prime Minister declared that Canada would not permit the pollution or artificial deterioration of the Arctic environment, either in the name of freedom of the seas or in the interests of economic development. He emphasized that we were determined not to bow in the Arctic to pressures of any state. With respect to the course of action proposed by the government he said:
Canada will propose a policy of use of the Arctic waters which will be designed for environmental preservation. This will not be an intolerable interference with the activities of others, it will not be a restriction upon progress. This legislation we regard, as a contribution to the long term and sustained development of resources for economic and social progress.
The special objectives we intend to achieve are known. The concrete action we intend to take will be spelled out in the legislation soon to be submitted to the House. I can assure the House that our proposed legislation will afford the protection required for Canada's vital coastal interests in the Arctic. It will not be a sterile exercise in chauvinism, blindly disregarding Canada's real interests and international responsibilities. It will, however, represent an affirmation of our right and our duty to use and control our national heritage. And it will vest in Canada the maritime jurisdiction which is essential for this purpose.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian north is beginning to undergo a period of rapid and profound change. We are disturbing its eternal silence and challenging its forbidden empti-
January 22, 1970

ness. At the same time, we are creating new problems and seeking to resolve them in new ways, with new techniques, new attitudes and new laws. The future of the north is the future of this country. The government is dedicated to that future, to the development of the north and to its preservation from the ravages which man has inflicted upon his environment elsewhere.

I hope it does not mean what the government usually means when it says "in the near future", that is, next year or the year after. I hope the assurance will be given in the next couple of weeks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the contents of this


report, which I hope at least in principle will have the support of every member of this House, I wish to place on record some of the background of the report.
The Arctic sovereignty question was raised and pursued in this House at the beginning of 1969 by the hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre). As a result of that hon. member's opportune action, the Indian Affairs and Northern Development Committee took up the subject and last April heard expert testimony from Dean Cohen of the McGill University faculty of law.
In August, 1969, when the timetable for the Manhattan became fixed, the committee indicated its wish to welcome the Manhattan to the Canadian north. This fact is significant, Mr. Speaker: the committee was in consequence furnished with a Canadian Armed Forces' aircraft for that purpose. The committee's primary concern was that our Arctic environment and ecology could be protected only by rules and regulations formulated and enforced by Canada.
The implementation of controls and regulations for the use of these waters is, of necessity, an exercise of sovereignty. The nature of the Manhattan's voyage, with no formal request for permission for its passage having been addressed to the Canadian government, at least in the minds of the committee members presented a challenge to Canadian sovereignty, a sovereignty which I regard as being solidly based historically, geographically and geologically.
We felt a strong gesture was essential to meet what seemed to be a deliberate attempt by the United States government to skate around the sovereignty issue. A subcommittee of 10 members of the Standing Committee went north on September 3, 1969, fully aware of the significance of the gesture they were about to make.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Soon after the committee arrived in Resolute on the evening of September 3, the ten members sat down together and in the course of the most completely non-partisan discussion I have ever witnessed between members of an all-party committee thrashed out not only the wording but the tone of the message of greeting we were to send to the Manhattan as she entered the waters of the archipelago. A condition of agreement on the wording of the message was that there would be unanimous support for the message after it had been delivered, and I am happy to say there was. The clearest possible language was used
January 22, 1970

to express the Canadian position: "Welcome to Canadian waters-Bienvenue dans ces eaux canadiennes".
Mr. Speaker, I am not an extreme nationalist, nor am I a flag-waver, nor do I believe in sovereignty for sovereignty's sake. However, 1 am totally convinced, as I know were the other nine members of the committee and as I believe are most hon. members of this House, that in order to regulate and control pollution dangers to our Arctic environment we must exercise the full sovereign powers of Canada.
Our report alludes to possible international control. We rejected a reliance on international regulations for protection because up to now, at least, their laxness has been such as to cause concern. Oil spillages, deliberate or accidental, have already reached an intolerable level in some of the temperate waters of the world, and these are the waters in which crude oil is dissipated most readily.
It is becoming increasingly clear to scientists that permissible levels of oil spillage under the present IMCO agreements may be much too high. The IMCO, as I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) found out during his voyage to Europe a short time ago, is dominated by countries whose shipping lobbies are very powerful. These shipping lobbies are in turn subservient to their most important clients, the international oil interests.
International agreement on stricter control of oil and chemical pollution by international marine traffic remains a highly desirable objective, and it is in the interest of Canada to use maximum diplomatic pressure to achieve these goals. But can we take a chance on the adequacy of international regulation when thousands of miles of Canadian Arctic coastline are menaced, and when an ecology and an environment which are probably the most delicately balanced on this planet may be irreparably damaged? The answer must, of course, be no.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already indicated that the government of Canada will take whatever steps are necessary to protect the Arctic environment in this regard. The committee has made clear what it feels these steps should be. It states that vessels, surface and submarine, passing through Canada's Archipelago are, and shall be, subject to the sovereign control and regulation of Canada.
The urgency which is stressed in the committee's report is not exaggerated. A few 21611-33)
Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
days ago General Dynamics Corporation announced it had offered to build six 175,000-ton submarine tankers for oil companies with interests in the Prudhoe Bay area. The offer was made complete with prices and delivery dates. I asked in the House the day after it was announced, and I ask now, whether this company has consulted with anyone in the Canadian government on the subject. I suspect the answer is no. Canada, and Canada alone, must determine whether surface or submarine maritime traffic can be safely tolerated in the Arctic Archipelago. All of us hope it can, but it is Canada's sovereign prerogative to decide whether the answer shall be yes or no, to declare one design satisfactory and another unsatisfactory.
I should like to ask the minister responsible for the National Research Council just what assessment and evaluation capacity we possess in Canada which would enable us to decide independently which surface or submarine vessel design is acceptable or unacceptable. I can assure the minister responsible for the NRC that some time within the next few months our committee will want to hear from the NRC just how Canada is prepared to evaluate the safety of these proposed gigantic surface and submarine oil tankers.
Returning briefly to the report, I should like to comment on two points which apart from the sovereignty recommendations I deem to be the most important. The committee believes that innocent passage for ships of all nations should not be interfered with. It states clearly:
The committee believes that innocent passage for ships of ail nations through the waters of the Canadian Archipelago is compatible with the protection of fundamental and essential Canadian interests in her Arctic waters. However, the committee takes the position that any passage which poses a danger to Canada whether this danger takes the form of a threat of pollution or otherwise, is not innocent.
We have here simply taken the realistic position that any ship from any nation can use this passage as long as it does not threaten Canada. If an unsafe ship is using the passage, it is threatening Canada and Canada has an absolute right to control it.
The second point I want to stress is this: the committee urged the government to take whatever steps might be necessary, compatible with international law, to deal with this problem in the Arctic. It is significant that the committee used the phrase "compatible with international law", and I draw the attention of the House to this.
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic
I should also like to place on record my position with regard to the motion presently before us. I, of course, support the motion.

speechtext:
Why then, Mr. Speaker, did I not move concurrence as chairman? The opposition knows, as does everyone else here, that I was not so instructed by the committee and that the practice, until the ruling of Mr. Speaker on Tuesday, was that a committee chairman did not move concurrence without an explicit direction from the committee.
I do not think I am breaking any rule if I say that during the three committee meetings which were held in camera, the members of all parties represented in the House and present at the meeting held to consider this question stressed again and again the delicacy of the sovereignty issue and the importance of avoiding phraseology which might lend itself to deliberate misinterpretation on the part of various interests opposed to the assertion and exercise of Canadian sovereignty over the water of our Arctic Archipelago.
Its objective was to put on record, not only for the government of Canada but for foreign governments, a unanimous, all-party expression of concern with regard to the imminent oil-pollution danger facing Canada's Arctic environment. There was an equally unanimous conviction and recommendation that the government of Canada should act urgently to indicate to the world-and I am repeating what the recommendation said-that shipping, surface and submarine, passing through these waters is subject to the sovereign control and regulation of Canada.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker's ruling of Tuesday last was a dramatic procedural development and one which I on balance support, although in this particular case it presents some very special difficulties for the government. Normally, if the government had any reservation about any part of a report it would vote against it. In this instance the government really does not have that opportunity, because a vote against this report would conceivably open the way for a foreign power to use this as proof that there exists some doubt in the government's mind as to whether we actually have sovereignty in that area. It is inconceivable that the government could vote against this report. In this particular case the government is more restricted than it otherwise would be.

I did not receive any instructions from the committee to move for concurrence and the question was not even raised in the committee by members of either the government or opposition parties. The progress which is implicit in the committees' system and which will be the result of the ruling on Tuesday augers well for the rights of backbenchers. We can only hope that the Committee on Procedure and Organization will heed the Speaker's recommendation that immediate consideration be given to developing-I do not think the Speaker used these precise words-guidelines for committee reports. From now on chairmen will move for concurrence in their reports as soon as they are presented; they will not wait around for opposition members to move concurrence. This is very obvious. However, we will be faced with new problems in respect of time allocation. I strongly urge the committee on Procedure and Organization to heed the Speaker's recommendation in this regard.
