speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the members of the northern affairs committee I considered we were asked to make recommendations affecting 40 per cent of Canada's land mass comprised of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Because many members of the committee had never been there, we decided to fly to Resolute and at least look at part of this area. This land is so vast that many rivers and lakes are nameless. It is a land of muskeg, permafrost and in some areas perpetual ice.
Along the fringes of the Arctic icecap marine life abounds. There is plankton, tiny Crustacea, fish, seals and polar bear. On land the caribou and muskox in their thousands
January 22, 1970

feed on the Arctic moss. Lemmings, the Arctic fox and hare are part of the scene. It is a land where winter holds sway for nine months of the year and where men fear the bone-snapping cold.
For centuries men have tried to force the Northwest Passage or otherwise explore the Arctic. It was necessary to await the technology of the 20th century to properly assess this vast area. With the advent of the aeroplane, helicopter, Bombardier and huge icebreakers, transportation in the north has become a reality. Even yet, however, it is fabulously expensive.
Geologists suggest that there is more of the sedimentary-type rock in the Arctic than there is in Alberta and Saskatchewan. This includes the tarsands discovery on Melville Island. Rich deposits of iron on Baffin Island await development. I saw with my own eyes samples of ore with free gold and silver showing in them. The key to this storehouse of natural resource is transportation.
The trip of the Manhattan is now history, but history will not stop here. There is more to come. I should like to read a short item from a newspaper quoting Yellowknife as the source. It states:
Prime Minister Trudeau should declare Canadian sovereignty over the waters surrounding the Arctic islands, the Northwest Territories council agreed yesterday.
The council also expressed concern over Arctic pollution, and requested Territorial Commission Stuart Hodgson to seek a means of having representation at any pollution talks between Canada and the United States.
"Occupancy is nine-tenths of the law," said Duncan Pryde, sponsor of the resolution asking the council to support a federal standing committee on Indian affairs and northern development recommendation for Canadian sovereignty in the Arctic.
We have the approval of the commission in the Northwest Territories, or at least part of that group, in this regard. We have at least caught the eyes of some of the people responsible for government in that area. This is a voice to which we should listen. The article then states:
Mr. Pryde, elected member for the Western Arctic, said Canadian Eskimos have occupied sea ice between the Islands for centuries.
"These are Canadian Eskimos, not American Eskimos or international Eskimos," he said.
1 suggest that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a political mistake when he did not speak out firmly on this issue when it first came up. Had he done so, the argument we have heard several times in the last few

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic months would not have been made. I think, too, that the Prime Minister made a political mistake in the sense that this is one issue in respect of which he might have the support of all Canadians. The fact that the members of the committee from all parts of Canada were unanimous in agreement on this subject indicates that there is unanimity among Canadians on this subject. The Prime Minister missed the boat on this matter.
It would appear that the United States is challenging us on this issue. Why does it not challenge the Russians about the Russian sector of the Arctic? Why does the United States not ask the Russians whether that sector of the Arctic waters is open to international transportation? I suggest the answer is that they know it is not, and dare not ask.
I do not want to belabour the point about the continental shelf because it has already been made today, but I have an item from which I would like to read briefly. This is to be found in The Canadian Forum in an article on Arctic sovereignty. It states in part:
The first principle is the concept of the continental shelf. The second is the utilization of straight "baselines" to designate the limits of the domestic or internal waters of a state. The continental shelf doctrine achieved prominence in 1945 when President Truman proclaimed that the resources of the subsoil and seabed of the continental shelf adjacent to a country's shore belong to that nation.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
This principle was incorporated in an international convention at the United Nations Geneva Conference on the Law of the Sea in 1958.
I shall leave it at that. The reason I mention this matter is that it is one the United States authorities have promoted. They have promoted this idea, and that is one reason for claiming this area for Canada. I suggest it is not enough for the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development or the Prime Minister to declare that these waters are ours. This should be demonstrated by a more visible Canadian presence in the area.
Duncan Pride of the Northwest Territories Commission suggested that occupancy is nine-tenths of the law. I suggest this is the way the United States authorities consider the issue. If we were to look at Oregon in an historical sense, one might argue that it should be part of British America. The Americans moved into this area and because of the right of occupancy it became part of the United States. A similar thing happened in respect of California and New Mexico.
If the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) believes the United States people are
January 22, 1970

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic always fair in dealing with their good neighbour to the north, he should read Bruce Hutchison's book "Struggle for the Border". In that book he would see what Mr. Hutchison has to say concerning the argument about the Alaska panhandle. I do not think the hon. member would then be so happy about this situation. I suggest the Canadian presence could take the form of Canadian icebreakers, merchant ships and naval ships using these waters. Accurate charts of water depths, currents and ice movements should be made. Navigational aids should be installed and kept operational. Bases should be enlarged and expanded. The larger ones should be converted to family-type communities with houses, schools, and so on. In this way we would in effect be saying: We are here now, to stay.
For the immediate present the armed forces might demonstrate a visible presence. Troops returning from NATO exercises could profitably learn how to navigate and manoeuvre in Canada's conditions of ice, tundra, muskeg, mosquitoes, mountains, and so on. The navy could learn how to navigate in Arctic ice and winter conditions.
I feel it is regrettable that the government with the northern vision in 1958 decided to stop naval patrol of the Arctic. I think that had we had continuous naval patrols in the Arctic we might now be more operational in respect of safeguards for the ships we have there. We might also have completed our study of the area, for which there is need. I think it is regrettable that we do not have a constant naval program there now.
I did not hear the interjection of the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange), but I would ask him what our navy is doing patrolling the Caribbean when it does not know how to manoeuvre in Canadian waters. I would suggest, in dealing with Arctic sovereignty, that perhaps our Air Force transport services should be updated. The army engineers might be used to build temporary wharf facilities, airports, and so on. I recall ships being unloaded at Resolute Point. They were 200 or 300 yards out in the harbour and barges were being used to transfer supplies to shore. I wonder whether the army might have provided a more reasonable type of wharf facility in this area. Perhaps it would be of a temporary type, but it would be more effective than the facilities there at the time of our visit.
These are our suggestions. Perhaps there is some argument about their effectiveness. At

any rate, they are my opinions. I believe the facilities would be useful and that the army would pick up some useful experience in northern conditions. Armed forces reserve units might spend some time in the Arctic on a rotating basis, perhaps taking the Arctic survival course as part of their training. These bases, communities, mines, oil companies, and so on, are in a particularly exposed position in respect of supplies in the event of international turmoil. Therefore, I believe these waters should be treated as inland waters and that freight should be restricted to Canadian shipping only.
Freighters for this service should be equipped for navigating and plowing through ice. They should also have rapid unloading facilities and equipment for cold weather. Much of the cold weather equipment is inadequate. Clothing, weapons, lubricating oil, engines, metals, ships, and so on, could be improved. Therefore, the Department of National Defence in co-operation with the Department of Northern Affairs, the National Research Council and industries concerned should be encouraged to continue research into improved services in these areas.
I should like to stress one point which I believe was made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) this evening. I refer to the fact that we do not need to hesitate standing up for ourselves regarding shipping in these waters, because ships of other countries cannot use them without our support services. The land around these waters is ours. If there should be any pollution there, our land would be polluted. For this reason, also, we should take firm action. If there are military ships in this area, whether of a friendly or less friendly nation, Canada either directly or indirectly should exert all its authority to make certain nothing untoward happens and then, whether we like it or not, we will be involved.
I realize there are other members who wish to speak. I do not wish to labour my points, and therefore I shall yield the floor.

speechtext:
During the course of the debate this afternoon and evening I could not help being impressed, as a northerner living in the south at the moment, by the sincerity with which Canadians and Members of Parliament who represent many other people in this country expressed concern about northern Canada. Probably there is no issue today in the minds of the Canadian people that reflects more greatly the true feelings of nationhood in this country than the question of Arctic sovereignty.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I believe we have finally recognized that this is a nation which does not stretch from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but from the Atlantic to the Arctic and on to the Pacific. Less than 20 years ago the islands of the Arctic Archipelago were a mysterious and forbidding land which concerned Canadians not at all and interested them even less.
Following the start of the Dew Line, the Distant Early Warning System, somewhere around 1953, and with the changes which governments have brought about since then, including the establishment of the Department of Northern Affairs, this massive land mass in the north and the people who live there are now truly a part of the Canadian conscience.
This year we in the north are celebrating our 100th year in the Canadian Confederation. In 1870 the government of Canada bought back Ruperts Land from Britain, an area which included the present provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and all of the Northwest Territories. For 80

Canadian Sovereignty in the Arctic years the northern part of that land continued to lie dormant. But in the last 20 years the people of Canada, through their government, have participated in the life of the north to make it truly part of our nation. In the north there is a feeling that the Canadian Confederation is the most important thing to us as Canadians. It is finally apparent to northerners that the people who live in southern Canada are concerned about the north.
This is demonstrated by the manner in which Members of Parliament talk about the north and ask that more emphasis be placed on northern development. This area north of the 60th parallel comprises more than 40 per cent of our land mass, but has a very small population. Hopefully, it holds those resources that will make this country truly Canadian in the years to come.
Today we are spending some time debating the question of Arctic sovereignty. What do we do about it? What do we do about the passage through Lancaster Sound, Barrow Strait, and the Prince of Wales Strait to make sure that we as Canadians have a right to say which ships can pass, and can control them so they will not destroy the tender but vital life of the Arctic?
As members of Parliament we face a dilemma. We could unilaterally say-emotionally I believe we should, although intellectually I am not too sure-that these are Canadian waters. We could display our jingoism and all the other things which make headlines. But how do we do it effectively? Do we suddenly stand up and say that all these waters belong to Canada?

I believe in the sovereignty of this country. We have established our sovereignty on the islands. We have established sovereignty on the polar shelf. We also control the only Northwest Passage there is, between Banks Island and Victoria Island through the Prince of Wales Strait because of the two islands known as the Princess Royal Islands, which he in this area and which are Canadian territory. To try and sail any other way is impossible. If a ship goes beyond Banks Island it hits the polar ice pack, and there is no way the Manhattan or even a bigger ship can get through the polar ice pack.
As Canadians we control the Northwest Passage. It is ours. We can say which ships can pass through it. We can set the standards. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record, in support of my concern about the United States approach to this whole matter, a document written by Mr. Howard W. Pollock, Congressman for the State of Alaska, to the chairman of the House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries, the Hon. Edward A. Garmatz, Member of the House of Representatives. This document is a matter of public record and it is a report of Mr. Pollock's trip on the Manhattan. I think it is an indication of the lack of recognition on the part of our neighbours to the south of the use, control and ownership of these waters. I think it is a matter that should concern all Canadians. I shall not read the entire letter, which is rather long. The first paragraph deals with the trip into Alaskan waters and the second paragraph reads as follows:
Unquestionably the s.s. Manhattan is the largest, most powerful Icebreaker in the world, and it performed spectacularly under most rigorous ice conditions. It sliced through enormous ice pressure ridges up to an estimated forty to sixty feet in height with no roll, no sway, and no shudder. The powerful ship outperformed the escorting Canadian and United States Coast Guard icebreakers. The performance exceeded all expectations. ALLEGED MISLEADING ADVERTISING BY IMPERIAL TOBACCO COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hoped that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) would be in his place this evening because I wish to bring before this House a matter of concern to all Canadians and of particular interest to the minister and his department. I hope his absence does not indicate a lack of concern, because I am sure the minister is well aware of the issue being debated this 21611-341
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion evening; I am certain that he was given notice of it.
The problem I wish to raise is posed by certain forms of advertising and sales promotion which tend to mislead consumers. The majority of these advertisements and promotional stunts may be so carefully phrased as to be within the limits of legality. However, regardless of how they are worded and presented to the public, the end result is to mislead the consumer in varying degrees.
I first raised this matter in the form of a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on January 15. The question was in reference to recent events which occurred in Alberta. These events evolved from the promotion of a new brand of cigarette, Casino, by the manufacturers, the Imperial Tobacco Company of Canada Limited. By means of advertising, consumers were invited to buy Casino cigarettes and thereby have a chance of winning cash prizes by playing a game called Casino, details of which were enclosed in each package.
It is not my intention this evening to go into detail about the rules and method of play. It will suffice to say that a number of consumers who bought the product and played the game according to company rules are still waiting for the promised prize payment. In some cases these claims for payment amount to as much at $20,000 or $30,000. It is not my intention to make a charge that the advertising was either false or misleading in its origin and early application. However, I do say that it becomes both false and misleading the moment the manufacturer-fails to honour claims for prizes won in accordance with the rules as advertised.
Furthermore, I submit that it becomes very questionable when an organization spends huge sums of money on advertising and promoting not only the cigarette but the game, through television, radio and newspaper and then finds itself in a position of having to withdraw from the game and does so simply by placing a small and insignificant advertisement on the back pages of the daily newspapers.
This may not constitute misleading advertising, but I strongly suggest that it constitutes a deprivation of information to the public and consumer, particularly to those who bought these cigarettes in good faith on the strength of the company's advertising and adhered to the rules and regulations that were stated on the package. The rules which
January 22, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion were quoted stated that prize claims must be postmarked no later than July 31, 1970, in one series and in another series indicated that the deadline for claiming a prize was December 31, 1971.
I submit that actions of this sort do very little to dispel the anxieties and apprehensions of caveat emptor. This is clearly a matter within the jurisdiction of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
My understanding is that some time after the new brand was launched in the Alberta market, the company discovered a flaw in the game of Casino that made it possible for buyers to win more easily and to win greater amounts of money than had been anticipated.
I believe that on December 4 the product was withdrawn from the market and all promotion ceased. On December 13, Alberta newspapers carried advertisements announcing this and stating that the company would honour no applications for prize money if they were dated after December 12.
I would also point out, Mr. Speaker, that notwithstanding the fact that the company announced withdrawal of the product from the market, it was still available in retail outlets in Smoky Lake, Alberta, as late as January 9, 1970.
It is my understanding that one or more of these claims will shortly be contested in the courts. In any event, many consumers in Alberta believe they have just claims for prize money which have not been satisfied. I cite this as an example of the type of thing that is happening in many fields involving consumer affairs. It is my firm conviction that this aspect of consumer affairs should be of prime interest to the minister and to his department whose chief job, we have been told, it is the protection of the interests of the Canadian consumer.
Far be it from me to say that the company in this case is necessarily at fault. I do say, however, that the circumstances are such as to fully warrant a thorough and complete investigation by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. If this department is not prepared to initiate an investigation, it might well be a matter for the Department of Justice to deal with. I understand from the questions and answers in the House yesterday that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and the officials of his department are familiar with this matter.
Advertising is the chief method of promoting sales to consumers and moving consumer


goods. It is obvious, to me at least, that it should therefore be one of the main areas of interest to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I believe the question I raise tonight clearly falls within the department's jurisdiction, and I urge the minister to meet the challenge by examining this and similar matters at once.

SPORTS-FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR OLYMPIC GAMES BIDS
speechtext:
May I at the outset, Mr. Speaker, congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), and indeed his entire staff, on their positive and constructive approach to Canadian sports development and physical fitness.
Assigned these responsibilities a relatively short time ago, the minister and his staff have established an excellent record. My question relates to the amount of aid which has, in fact, been pledged by the federal government to the sponsors of Canada's Winter Olympic Games application and the amount of aid, if any, pledged by the government to the sponsors of the Montreal Summer Olympic Games application. I suggest that some urgency exists and we must have the facts. The picture is confused, and contradictory statements have been made which do nothing to assist either application.
As hon. members know, both in the Van-couver-Garibaldi winter games bid and the bid by Montreal for the summer games relate to events scheduled for 1976. However, right now, this very day, representatives of the International Olympics Commission are, I am advised, examining the bids within their national organizations in preparation for the critical vote which will take place in Amsterdam on May 13.
It is no secret that only extraordinary circumstances permit a country to bid successfully for both the winter and the summer Olympic Games. Canada has established an outstanding reputation for winter sports facilities. The mountains of western Canada
January 22, 1970

were built-to-order for the winter Olympics competition. The Vancouver-Garibaldi Olympics Commission has worked tirelessly since its establishment in 1960 to bring the winter games to the west.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
There have been keen disappointments along the way. Their 1961 bid was rejected because of lack of road facilities. In 1966 the provincial government opened a paved access road. The obstacles have been cleared away and Garibaldi is ready.
A remarkable amount of co-operation has been realized. Together with the enthusiastic support of the sports community there has been widespread citizen support as well as pledges of financial support from both federal and provincial governments. Until recently all indicators pointed to a successful Vancouver-Garibaldi bid. All Canada was convinced that this nation had a good chance to win the winter Olympic Games and that the games would be held at Whistler Mountain in the Garibaldi area.
However, Mayor Drapeau of Montreal elected to enlist the support of public opinion for the summer Olympic Games in Montreal in 1976 by making statements to the public through the media-statements, Mr. Speaker, which I suggest may not represent the facts and indeed could be very damaging to Canada's bid for the winter games.
I respect the enthusiasm and energy of Mayor Drapeau, but the eyes of the sports world are on Canada and it is vitally important to Canada's prestige as a winter wonderland that the Vancouver-Garibaldi Olympic Committee receive the support of all Canada-the kind of overwhelming support that all Canada gave to Expo '67 in Montreal.
In the Montreal Gazette dated January 15, 1970, on the front page a full-column story appears, part of which reads as follows:
Mr. Drapeau appeared both confident Montreal will win the games and convinced the city is fully capable of hosting them.
The impression left with readers clearly was that he had the blessing and support of the federal government. I am advised that the same gentleman also spoke to members of the Olympic Games officials in terms which left little doubt he had been assured of federal government support. In competitions of this kind support usually means financial grants. It is therefore vital to Canada's success in its bid for the winter games that the record be put straight, without delay.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Because of the excellent facilities already available at the Whistler Mountain area, the Vancouver-Garibaldi competition will have a net cost of $25 million and I am advised that the federal government has graciously agreed to pay a portion of this cost. I am advised that the Olympic Summer Games in Montreal could cost a minimum of $200 million, and possibly up to $300 million. There may be a time in the future when an expenditure of this magnitude could be justified. If such is the case, I am confident that I can assure Mayor Drapeau he will receive the wholehearted support of Canadians. But, Mr. Speaker, there can surely be no justification for making a commitment at this time.
The Vancouver-Garibaldi Olympic Committee's bid for the Winter Olympic Games in 1976 is a "first" for Canada. It will provide a meeting place for young people from all over the world generally and from all over Canada in particular. People from the Canadian east will visit the west in droves, as those from the west visited the east in Montreal during Expo '67.
In closing, may I express to the federal government the sincere gratitude of Canadian winter sportsmen from coast to coast for its support in assuring a successful bid being made by the Vancouver-Garibaldi Olympic Committee.

maintopic: SPORTS-FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR OLYMPIC GAMES BIDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) on January 15 concerning federal financial commitments for Montreal and Garibaldi in support of their bids for the 1976 Olympic Games, I would like to say that Montreal did not request direct financial assistance and therefore no commitment has been given to them. It is understood, however, that Montreal will be seeking indirect financial support under either existing legislation or legislation that might exist in the future concerning urban renewal and public housing. It is understood that any costsharing program applied for would have to be justified in its own right without consideration of its association with the Olympic Games.
In the case of the Vancouver-Garibaldi bid, the federal government was asked to participate financially and the federal government has agreed to a grant of $75,000 to help defray their promotional expenses in further-
January 22, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ing the bid. That represents one-third of the total promotional money. The other two-thirds have been supplied by the province of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver.
The federal government has further agreed to provide a fixed grant of $10 million toward the deficit of a non-profit corporation to be established for the staging and operation of the games. This grant is conditional upon the corporation obtaining from the government of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver an undertaking in terms acceptable to the federal government that either or both the government of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver will pay the balance of the deficit of the corporation, and that the federal government be satisfied that adequate provision has been made for the recognition of its role in the promotion and staging of the games and in the ceremonials and elements of publicity employed in connection with them.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the city of Montreal did not initially apply for and has not received from the federal government a grant for the purposes of staging the Olympic Games; nor has the city of Montreal to date applied for funds from any other government cost-sharing program in relationship to the Olympic Games. The city of Vancouver applied for assistance, and if the aforementioned conditions are met, will receive an outright grant of $10 million for the purposes of staging the 1976 Olympic Games.
